NRM SUCCESSION TALKS: CLARIFYING THE POSITION ON GEN MUHOOZI KAINERUGABA.

By Keefa Nuwahereza.
Uganda’s ruling National Resistance Movement is navigating intensifying discussions about political succession as President Yoweri Museveni, now in his early eighties and in power since 1986, approaches the later years of his current term that runs until 2031. At the centre of these conversations stands General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the Chief of Defence Forces and Museveni’s son, who has publicly signalled interest in contesting the presidency in the subsequent cycle. Recent weeks have produced a series of reports, clarifications and circulating documents that together illustrate the sensitivity of the issue inside the party.

In late October 2026, Museveni presented senior NRM leaders with a discussion paper outlining considerations for choosing a successor. According to accounts of that meeting, the paper suggested that Kainerugaba possessed relevant credentials in areas such as patriotism, Pan-Africanism, military leadership and commitment to the movement’s historical objectives. Some party figures later described this as an endorsement of sorts, while others characterised it as the opening of a structured conversation rather than a final decision. The paper itself has not been released publicly, leaving observers to rely on secondary accounts from participants and officials close to the process.

These discussions resumed on 10 November 2026 at a closed-door session of the NRM’s Central Executive Committee at State House Entebbe. Multiple media outlets, citing anonymous participants, reported that a proposal to position Kainerugaba as the party’s preferred successor was examined. According to those sources, a formal vote was begun but then abandoned after several members raised concerns. The accounts variously mentioned questions about Kainerugaba’s political experience outside the military, the tone of some of his public statements, and the advisability of first placing him in a civilian role to broaden his administrative exposure. One version indicated that only a minority of the roughly 28-member committee had cast ballots before the process was halted, with a narrow split among those who voted. The party has not released minutes or an official summary of the session.

On 12 November, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong issued a public statement addressing the circulating reports. He described claims that the committee had rejected a bid to position Kainerugaba as Uganda’s next president as “completely false.” Todwong noted that the Central Executive Committee routinely meets to discuss political, social and economic matters affecting the country and stated that any decisions reached would be communicated through official channels at the appropriate time. He urged the public to disregard online reports that had not been released by the party. Similar denials of active resistance came from figures associated with the Patriotic League of Uganda, the political movement linked to Kainerugaba, who maintained that the general’s ambitions had not encountered organised opposition within NRM structures.

In the days surrounding these events, various documents and images purporting to be official NRM press statements have circulated on social media. One such image, shared by accounts describing themselves as news outlets, claimed that the Central Executive Committee had unanimously endorsed Kainerugaba as the party’s presidential flag bearer and resolved to appoint him Vice President first as a transitional step. The language, formatting and signature block of that document closely resembled standard NRM stationery, yet it has not been confirmed by the party’s verified channels or by Todwong’s subsequent clarification. Official communications have focused on correcting what the party describes as inaccurate accounts of rejection rather than announcing an affirmative endorsement or timetable for a transition.

Kainerugaba’s own public posture has added further texture. He has stated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031 and has led mobilisation efforts through the Patriotic League of Uganda. In early November he also made remarks on social media suggesting that the current Vice President should prepare to vacate the office, remarks that drew attention amid the broader succession conversation. Supporters highlight his record as army chief, earlier command of the Special Forces Command, and efforts associated with anti-corruption messaging. Critics, including some within party circles according to the reported meeting accounts, have questioned whether military experience alone is sufficient preparation and have expressed concern about the implications of a father-to-son transition for institutional norms.

The wider context is one of a dominant ruling party that has governed since the mid-1980s and a president who has repeatedly amended constitutional term limits to remain in office. Museveni’s current mandate extends to 2031, after which a new election is scheduled. The absence of a clear, publicly articulated succession plan has long been a feature of Ugandan politics; the recent formalisation of discussion papers and committee meetings represents a shift toward more explicit internal deliberation. At the same time, the reliance on anonymous sourcing for details of the 10 November meeting, combined with the party’s refusal to confirm or deny specific outcomes beyond rejecting the “rejection” narrative, leaves substantial uncertainty about the balance of opinion inside the Central Executive Committee.

Observers note several possible pathways. One is a gradual elevation of Kainerugaba through civilian political roles, potentially including the vice presidency, while he remains or steps back from active military command. Another is continued delay, with Museveni remaining the party’s candidate should he choose to stand again and with succession deferred until after 2031. A third is internal contestation that remains unresolved for some time, given the reported differences of view. None of these scenarios has been officially selected. The party’s consistent message is that it will communicate decisions through established channels when they are ready.

For Uganda, the stakes include continuity of policy direction, the relationship between civilian and military institutions, and public confidence in the eventual transfer of power. Supporters of a managed transition argue that early clarity can reduce uncertainty and preserve stability. Others contend that open competition within the party, rather than designation of a preferred successor, better aligns with democratic principles and reduces the risk of factionalism. International partners have historically followed Uganda’s internal political processes closely because of the country’s role in regional security, refugee hosting and economic integration in East Africa.

As of mid-November 2026, the factual record consists of Museveni’s earlier discussion paper, reports of an inconclusive Central Executive Committee meeting on 10 November, and an official denial that any rejection of Kainerugaba’s potential role took place. No verified public announcement of an endorsement or of a concrete transitional arrangement has been issued by the NRM leadership. Circulating materials that claim otherwise have not been authenticated by the party. The next formal communication from the Secretary General or the National Chairman will therefore be the most reliable indicator of the direction the movement has settled upon. Until then, the succession conversation remains active, contested in its details, and unfinished.

The biggest sex symbol of the ’90s Anna Nicole Smith is in absolutely unbelievable shape in this fucking video I just found - every curve on full display. Playboy’s Playmate of the Year, the face of Guess, and at 26 the bride of an 89-year-old oil billionaire who left her fighting for $88 million. Here she’s 34, about to let reality show cameras into her home 24 hours a day. The bathroom was the only place off-limits - until she forgot to switch off her microphone in there. The entire crew heard everything.

She never looked like the other models of her decade. While everyone else was rail-thin, she was soft, curvy and unapologetically glamorous - and the world couldn’t look away. In 1993 Playboy crowned her Playmate of the Year. Guess put her on billboards. A year later she married J. Howard Marshall II - 89 years old, worth a fortune. 14 months later he was gone, and she spent the next decade fighting his family for the money.

Then came the reality show.

E! offered her a show with cameras following her every second. She didn’t think twice. “I was like, okay, just go for it.” She didn’t ask about sleep, showers or privacy - she just said yes.

Seven weeks into filming, she sat down on a talk show to talk about it - and admitted the worst part.

The bathroom. The one room the cameras weren’t allowed into. One day she went in - and forgot her microphone was still on. The crew heard everything. “I was really embarrassed.”

The hosts couldn’t stop laughing. She laughed along.

The show premiered on August 4, 2002 - exactly 7 years to the day after her husband died - and pulled the highest cable ratings ever for a reality debut. That same year a judge awarded her $88 million from his estate.

But even that day, one detail stuck. Her son hated the cameras in their house. Four years later he was gone, just days after she welcomed her baby daughter - and five months after that, Anna Nicole Smith died at 39. Under that video today, the most-liked comments aren’t about her body or the scandals. They say she still seemed innocent and sweet. And that hopefully, she and Daniel are finally together, in peace.

Slim and famous or curvy and real - which Anna was hotter?

👶🏻👶🏽👶🏿 Newborn Day 15 to 21, Infant Week 3: First Growth Spurt
Moms, Book 2, Infant Education, covers 68 of the 70 phonograms your child needs to learn to read. This week, many newborns hit their first growth spurt and want to feed all the time. What else changes in Week 3?
🎥 Two Videos This Week
Video 1: Guardian Angel Ara sings this week's song, gentle baby music for the third week home.
📚 Source: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). General information only; follow your pediatrician's advice for your own baby.
Video 2: the phonics lesson, RISE, FALL, and SPIRAL, sung slowly so your baby hears every sound. Phonic songs like these, with lullabies, nursery rhymes, and kids music, are the sound garden of a GLAL home.
🤖 AI disclosure: This phonics lesson was created with Grok AI.

📈 The First Growth Spurt
Around two to three weeks, many babies suddenly seem hungry all the time. They want to feed more often, sometimes every hour for part of the day, and they may be fussier than usual. This is often a growth spurt, and it usually settles in two or three days.
A growth spurt is not a sign that something is wrong with your milk or your baby. It is your baby's body asking for more because it is building more. When you answer by feeding, your body answers back by making more milk. This is God's design of supply and demand.
“And Jesus advanced in wisdom, and in age, and in grace, with God and men.” (Luke 2:52, CPDV)
“President George Washington was born February 22, 1732, in Westmoreland County, Virginia. He grew to about six feet two inches, unusually tall for his time, led the Continental Army, and became the first president of the United States.”

🩺 What Your Doctor Knows This Week
Pediatricians often describe growth spurts around two to three weeks, again around six weeks, and around three months. During a spurt, feed on cue. Unless your pediatrician advises it, a breastfed baby does not need formula added just because of a hungry day or two.
Spit-up is still common this week. A baby who spits up but is gaining weight and seems comfortable is often called a happy spitter. Forceful, projectile vomiting after feedings, especially between two and eight weeks, needs a call to your pediatrician the same day.

👀 What Your Baby Senses
Your baby may begin to follow a slow-moving face or a bold object for a moment, side to side. Your baby turns toward familiar voices and may calm at the sound of yours. If the newborn hearing screen needs a recheck, that recheck should happen by one month.

🧠 What the Psychologist Knows
Researchers call it parentese: a slow, sing-song way of talking with a higher pitch, stretched vowels, and lots of rising and falling melody. Studies show babies who hear more parentese at home tend to babble more and say more words later.

🤲 Holding and Carrying
Your baby's head is still heavy and the neck is still weak, so support the head every time you lift, carry, or hand your baby to someone. During tummy time, your baby may lift the head for a moment and turn it side to side. That is real work for a three-week-old.

🚨 When to Call Your Pediatrician
Call for forceful or projectile vomiting, green or bloody vomit, a baby who is too sleepy to feed, fewer wet diapers, a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, or a baby who seems to be in pain or will not be comforted. You know your baby best.

👣 Tummy Time This Week
Try tummy time on your chest while you lean back, or on a blanket on the floor, a few minutes at a time, several times a day. Talk and sing at eye level. Rising and falling melodies give your baby a reason to lift the head and look for you.

📝 Journal This Week
Write down the days of this growth spurt: how often your baby fed, how long it lasted, and how your body kept up. Note the first time your baby followed your face. These notes help you recognize the next spurt when it comes.

🎵 Keep Singing
This week, play with the melody of your voice. Sing baby music and lullabies high and low, slow and soft. Phonic songs and nursery rhymes carry rising and falling patterns that babies love. Your baby is learning the music of language before the words.

🔜 In the Deep Dive
The Deep Dive goes deeper into Week 3: growth spurts and feeding on cue, spit-up and when vomiting is serious, gas and stools, hearing and the speech melody called parentese, reading aloud, safe babywearing, mom's sleep and warning signs, and dad's role.

👶🏻👶🏽👶🏿 Infant Deep Dive: Week 3 (Days 15 to 21): First Growth Spurt
🙏 Built for Growth
Your baby was not made to stay small. From the first cell, God wrote growth into every part of your child. This week you can see it: tiny clothes already feel tight, and your baby's appetite says, more, more, more.
Growth spurts can feel like the hardest days so far. You may feel you do nothing but feed. Remember what is happening: your arms are holding a body that is building itself with every feeding. This is God's plan, and you are part of it.

🍼 Feeding Through a Growth Spurt
During a growth spurt, a breastfed baby may cluster feed for hours, especially in the evening. Offer the breast whenever your baby shows hunger cues. Within a day or two, your milk supply usually rises to meet the new demand, and feeding settles down.
Drink water whenever you sit down to feed, keep easy snacks within reach, and let someone else handle meals and chores. A growth spurt is a season for staying close, not for getting things done. The dishes can wait; this window will not.
Formula-fed babies go through growth spurts too. If your baby finishes every bottle and still roots and sucks hungrily, ask your pediatrician whether to offer a little more. Do not add extra powder or water to formula; always mix it exactly as the label says.
Signs the spurt is passing: your baby goes a little longer between feedings, sleeps a bit more, and seems content again. If the hungry, fussy days go on for more than a week, or wet diapers drop, call your pediatrician to check weight and feeding.

🫧 Spit-Up, Reflux, and Vomiting
Most babies spit up because the muscle between the food pipe and the stomach is still weak. It often looks like more than it is. Spit-up usually peaks around four months and fades by about the first birthday, as that muscle grows stronger.
To help, feed in a more upright position, burp during and after feedings, avoid overfeeding, and keep your baby upright for a short time after eating. Do not put your baby to sleep on the side or tummy to prevent spit-up. Back to sleep is still the rule.
Call your pediatrician if your baby is not gaining weight, refuses to eat, cries in pain during feedings, or has blood or green color in the spit-up. These can be signs of reflux disease or another problem your pediatrician can treat.
One condition to know: pyloric stenosis, a narrowing at the bottom of the stomach, usually appears between two and eight weeks. The baby vomits forcefully, often shooting across the room, and seems hungry right after. It is treatable, but it needs prompt care.
“The Lord your God is the strength in your midst; he will save. He will rejoice over you with gladness. In his love, he will be silent. He will exult over you with praise.” (Zephaniah 3:17, CPDV)
“Singer Dolly Parton was born January 19, 1946, in Locust Ridge, Tennessee, the fourth of twelve children. In 1995 she founded the Imagination Library, which has mailed more than 200 million free books to young children so families can read aloud from the start.”

💨 Gas and Grunting
Babies swallow air when they feed and cry, and young babies have trouble pushing gas through. Gentle help: burp often, lay your baby on the back and move the legs in a slow bicycle motion, or hold your baby tummy-down along your forearm while awake.
Many newborns grunt, groan, and turn red while passing stool or gas. This is often called grunting baby, and it is usually normal. Your baby is learning to relax the right muscles at the right time. Soft stools mean your baby is not constipated.

🧷 Stools This Week
Breastfed babies often have several soft, yellow stools a day in the early weeks. After about three to six weeks, some begin to go less often, even once every few days, and that can still be normal if the stool is soft when it comes.
Formula-fed babies usually have firmer, tan or yellow stools. Call your pediatrician if stools are hard and pebble-like, if there is blood in the stool, or if stools are white, gray, or chalky. Pale stools can be a sign of a liver problem that needs to be checked.

👂 Hearing and the Music of Speech
Your baby's hearing was tested before you left the hospital. If the result said refer or recheck, make sure the follow-up test happens by one month. Experts aim to finish hearing tests by one month, find any hearing loss by three months, and start help by six months.
Watch how your baby reacts to sound at home. A newborn startles at loud noises and quiets or turns toward familiar voices. If your baby never seems to react to sound, mention it to your pediatrician, even if the hospital screen was normal.
Parentese is not baby talk with silly words. It is real words, spoken slowly and warmly with a sing-song melody: Hel-lo, my sweet ba-by! Researchers at the University of Washington found that babies who hear more one-on-one parentese babble more and say more words later.
Talk to your baby face to face, at close range, with lots of eye contact. Pause after you speak, as if waiting for an answer. In a few weeks, your baby will start to answer with coos. Every conversation now is a rehearsal for the first word.
“Out of the mouths of babes and infants, you have perfected praise, because of your enemies, so that you may destroy the enemy and the revenger.” (Psalm 8:3, CPDV (8:2 KJV))
“Actor Shirley Temple was born April 23, 1928, in Santa Monica, California. She received a special Academy Award at age six as a child star, and as an adult she served as a United States ambassador to Ghana and to Czechoslovakia.”

📖 Reading Aloud From Birth
The American Academy of Pediatrics encourages parents to read aloud to their babies starting at birth. Your baby will not follow the story. What your baby takes in is your voice, the rhythm of the sentences, and the closeness of your body.
Choose books with big, bold pictures and simple, rhyming words. Board books, picture books, and the Bible all count. Read for a few minutes when your baby is calm and alert. When your baby looks away or fusses, close the book and try again later.

😴 Sleep in Week 3
Newborns spend about half their sleep in active sleep, when they twitch, grunt, smile, and breathe unevenly. They may even open their eyes or cry out briefly and then settle. If your baby is not truly awake, pause a moment before picking your baby up.
Learning the difference between active sleep and waking up helps your whole family rest. Watch, listen, and wait a minute. If your baby wakes fully and is hungry, feed. Keep night feedings dim and quiet, and lay your baby back down on the back.

🤱 Safe Babywearing
Carrying your baby in a sling or soft carrier keeps your baby close and frees your hands. Choose a carrier made for newborns and follow its weight limits. Your baby's face should always be visible, not covered by fabric or pressed into your body.
Keep your baby upright and snug, high enough on your chest to kiss the top of the head. The chin must stay off the chest so the airway stays open. Check often, and never cook, carry hot drinks, or bend at the waist while wearing your baby.
“And embracing them, and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them.” (Mark 10:16, CPDV)
“Track star Jesse Owens was born September 12, 1913, in Oakville, Alabama, the son of a sharecropper and the grandson of enslaved people. At the 1936 Olympics in Berlin, he won four gold medals.”

👩 Mom's Sleep and Recovery
Three weeks of broken sleep adds up. If you can, split the night with your partner: one handles the early hours while the other sleeps, then you switch. Even one four-hour stretch of sleep can lift your mood and help you think more clearly.
High blood pressure after birth, called postpartum preeclampsia, can appear up to six weeks after delivery, even if your pregnancy blood pressure was normal. Call your doctor or go to the emergency room for a severe headache, blurry vision, seeing spots, or sudden swelling of the face or hands.
Call your doctor for a breast that is red, hot, hard, and painful, especially with fever or chills. This can be mastitis, an infection that is treated with medicine. Keep feeding or pumping from that side unless your doctor says otherwise.

👨 Dad and the Family This Week
Dads can own a part of the day. Many fathers take bath time, the evening walk, or the first night feeding with a bottle of pumped milk or formula. Doing the same job every day builds skill and confidence, and your baby learns your hands and your voice.
Older brothers and sisters can be readers too. A preschooler can tell the baby about the pictures in a book; a school-age child can read a short story out loud. Brothers and sisters often sing kids music and nursery rhymes with more joy than anyone else in the house.

🎶 Rising and Falling Songs
Lullabies, nursery rhymes, and phonic songs are full of rising and falling melody, the same melody your baby hears in parentese. When you sing, let your voice climb up and float down. Your baby is learning that language has a shape.
Baby music in the background is pleasant, but your live voice is best. Recorded songs cannot pause and wait for your baby to answer. You can. Sing a line, wait, smile, and sing again. That back-and-forth is how kids music becomes conversation.

🏠 Patterns in the Everyday
At GLAL School, the three words are intuition, algorithm, and mathematics. A growth spurt is a lesson in all three. Intuition: you sense the change in your baby. Algorithm: hunger, feed, supply, growth. Mathematics: more feedings now, more milk tomorrow.
Every rising and falling song you sing is a pattern your baby's brain is learning to predict. Predicting patterns is the root of reading, music, math, and later, working well alongside an AI partner like Claude. This is God's plan, unfolding one week at a time.

📝 Journal This Week
Write the dates of the growth spurt and how you got through it. Record the first time your baby followed your face, the first book you read aloud, and the rising and falling song that made your baby's eyes go wide. Thank God for one small victory.

🔤 Phonics This Week: Rise, Fall, Spiral
After this lesson comes the phonics lesson for RISE, FALL, and SPIRAL, each broken into its phonograms (letters that stand for sounds). These are motion words. Rising and falling is the shape of a melody, the same shape your voice makes in parentese.
Sing RISE on a rising note and FALL on a falling note, then hum SPIRAL in a gentle circle of sound. You may add last week's REACH, GROW, and LISTEN as a review. Keep each session short, and stop when your baby gives break signals.

🕊️ A Prayer for the Third Week
Lord, as Jesus advanced in wisdom, and in age, and in grace, with God and men (Luke 2:52, CPDV), let our child grow in body, mind, and spirit. Give us strength for the hungry days and long nights. Fill our mouths with songs of praise, and our home with Your peace. Amen.

✅ Week 3 Checklist
• Feed on cue through the growth spurt
• Watch for projectile vomiting
• Burp during and after feedings
• Hearing recheck by one month if needed
• Read aloud a few minutes a day
• Talk in parentese, face to face
• Safe babywearing: face visible, chin up
• Mom watches for headache and vision changes
• Sing this week's song

🔜 Next Week
In Week 4, your baby turns one month old, and most babies have their one-month checkup. The phonics lesson moves on to FEEL, SENSE, and KNOW.

These words describe motion and shape — the visual patterns underneath music, breathing, and even thought itself. Rising and falling is the shape of a melody. A spiral is a rhythm that returns to itself, again and again, a little further along each time.

🧩 The Phonograms
r + ise = RISE
f + all = FALL
spi + ral = SPIRAL

🌱 Simple Words Today, Big Words Tomorrow
Rise and fall together become harmony. A spiral finds balance, and small motions align. In Book Three, Toddler Education, your child moves from these simple words to the complex words: harmony, balance, and align. Eager parents can start singing them now.

🎵 Try This Today
Sing RISE on a rising note and FALL on a falling note, then hum SPIRAL slowly in a gentle circular tone. Do it face to face in the quiet alert state, and stop when your baby gives break signals.

THE RECORD, DECLARED

IN THE ROYAL HOUSE OF GOOSE, November 14, 2026.
The Register Current of the Grievances of a Citizen of the United States of America

Every petition, inquiry, indictment, condemnation and damnation raised from this account, in the order raised, each beside its link, each declared on its own sources and quoted from the documents themselves. Read them whole.

"A decent respect to the opinions of mankind requires that they should declare the causes." They have been declared, one by one. Here they are, together.

"To prove this, let Facts be submitted to a candid world."

WHERE IT BEGAN

WE THE PEOPLE · https://t.co/iPLyJ0zPEH
Against all 535 seated members of the 119th Congress
Six FY2026 bills, the defense authorization among them, charged section by section for mandates that encroach on the President's powers under Article II. The governors and attorneys general asked to seek Supreme Court review; every State asked to investigate its delegation's backers for foreign influence. Closed on Washington's Farewell Address.
https://t.co/JiqZZtMvOW

THE PETITION, THE INQUIRY AND THE INDICTMENTS

THE PETITION · to the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, and to the Pope
For the unalienable rights of all peoples, "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness," raised in Latin by a lay member of the faithful, under canon 212. To the Dicastery: a doctrinal Note binding priests and prelates to put innocent human life before any temporal political end, and penal law for public, obstinate denial of Evangelium vitae 57. To the Pope: a common effort with the Eastern Churches to protect children born and unborn, and a worldwide review of Church property accounts.
https://t.co/UNnZwyrpQi

THE BANNER · A Citizen's Indictment and Condemnation
Against the ICC, the ICJ, the UN, the WTO, the EU, and the committees of Basel and Paris
Six counts, each set against the clause it offends. Our rights are not granted by government; they are fenced off from it. Then every time since 1919 the question was put and the Constitution answered it, even when our own Presidents were the ones asking.
https://t.co/NgTe8NVuBZ

BEFORE THE DAIS · An Inquiry
To the eight living Secretaries of State
Not a charge against any of them: a charge against what the office has been allowed to become, measured against the government's own auditors. Seven questions to all of them, and one to each on their own record.
https://t.co/pltubkVVeJ

IN CONGRESS ASSEMBLED · A Citizen's Indictment of the First Branch
Against the Senate and the House, under every majority that has held them
Nine counts of power abandoned: the purse let fall, war without a declaration since 1942, the legislative power parcelled out to the agencies, the Federal Reserve and Basel, a House grown to one member for every 761,169, the enforcement clauses left asleep. "He has abdicated Government here." Answer by the yeas and nays.
https://t.co/jAVsOSRHPl

ONE SUPREME COURT · A Citizen's Indictment of the Third Branch
Against the Court, and the Chief Justice who alone designates its secret benches
Ten counts on three duties: to check the branches, to judge between the States, to guard the sovereignty. Answer by judgment, in a case.
https://t.co/vywTIPdChv

THE ROUNDS

ROUND I · THE EU · The Exits Already Written
Twenty U.S.–EU agreements the Executive may end on written notice, read out of the State Department's own Treaties in Force: passenger-name records, terrorist-finance tracking, Europol, Galileo–GPS, air transport. The weighing is State's and Treasury's. The first of a round for every power that gets uppity with us.
https://t.co/smLQ4MK6jL

ROUND II · THE EBRD · The Door Already Written
A bank America paid for to build open markets, now pledging half its financing to green purposes and aligning every investment to a treaty America left. The bill comes to Washington. The profit stays in London. The door: written notice, six months, no vote, and the money back to the Treasury.
https://t.co/gvoLSgGDS6

ROUND III · FRANCE · From the Present Time and Forever
A damnation of the French Republic on its own signature to the treaties of 1778. Fourteen counts, 1775 to 2019, from help that came invoiced to NATO shown the door. Convicted once already, by Act of Congress in 1798. On the French state, not the French people.
https://t.co/WLkZcFFC8J

ROUND IV · BASEL · The Landlord
The Bank for International Settlements: immunity "in time of peace and in time of war," and not one duty owed in return. Ten counts, from looted gold banked to parent of the European Central Bank. Its only American paper is a 1948 receipt for Nazi gold. The way out is a letter and an empty chair.
https://t.co/2NGjtqLGlN

ROUND V · THE PRESS · The Megaphone and the Muzzle
Censorship, plus mass bullshit distribution. Eight counts against the owners, wires, platforms and fact-checkers: one script read in a hundred towns, headlines the documents never wrote, foreign sovereign money in the equity. None of the terms silences anyone. Read the four pages, then the primary sources.
https://t.co/hJMoseJ9i4

ROUND VI · CANADA · Forever Free and Open
A condemnation of Canada by its own Boundary Waters Treaty: navigation "forever … free and open." Twenty-five counts, 1777 to 2026. On the Canadian state, not the Canadian people. Beneath it: 58 agreements the Executive can end alone, and a ledger that still lists NAFTA.
https://t.co/05lsCoaLYA

ROUND VII · THE CROWN · Unfeeling Brethren
A damnation of the United Kingdom, in the words Congress struck from Jefferson's draught: forts kept after the peace, envoys sent home for meddling, a war debt unpaid since the 1930s. Britain only comes second because France exists. Beneath it: 141 exits, clause by clause.
https://t.co/B254o2kMkw

ROUND VIII · AUSTRALIA · The Gateway
Three tiers. A damnation of its government: Darwin's port leased beside our Marines to a Chinese-owned company. A condemnation of its failures: the Pacific lost to Beijing on its watch. And a hand to the Australian people: go bilateral, lock down Oceania with us. Beneath it: 71 exits, 39 the Executive's alone.
https://t.co/X4dPDZNnPM

ROUND IX · NATO AND THE UNION · Such Subsidiary Bodies
A damnation of NATO by its own fourteen articles, and of the European Union for the abuse of American good faith, trust and sacrifice. An alliance amended by communique, with about 62 percent of allied defence spending on us; a Union that overruled its own peoples and planted its system in our hemisphere. To the twenty-seven: the clause each gave away, and the two doors, Articles 48 and 50.
https://t.co/OOPEwpRluu

ROUND X · THE UN AND DAVOS · Such Other Functions
A damnation of the United Nations by its own Charter, and of the World Economic Forum beside it: a Human Rights Council seating the accused, a partnership no organ voted on, a Charter that opens "WE THE PEOPLES" and has come to treat them as human resources. Not against the Charter, nor the nations under it.
https://t.co/iB27hON7lF

ROUND XI · THE AMERICAS · The American Shield
The hemisphere read by its own papers: 760 agreements screened, 576 read whole. The rule of 1823, given treaty form at Havana in 1940, still in force and built without a door. Beneath it: 255 exits the President holds by notice, and 107 Senate-ratified treaties, by citation.
https://t.co/YOcsF8VHbH

ROUND XII · ISRAEL · An Ally in Name
A damnation of the State of Israel, held to its own word: a constitution promised by 1 October 1948 and never written, a Government its own courts convicted. Eleven counts, from an American ally bombed in its capital to the Liberty. On the Israeli state, not the Israeli people, and not on American Jews, who are Americans. Beneath it: 74 agreements read for their exits.
https://t.co/GH1EPHFmce

ROUND XIII · CANADA · The Interests of the British Empire
A petition for the free peoples of Canada, and for the Americas. To the people: the Crown, the Company and the Bank, from the charter of 1670 to Montreal, 2026, where Ottawa put "an ever-closer association" with the Union in writing; and what is still theirs, a Constitution that outranks every pact and has no door to Brussels. To Washington: our word since 1823, our instruments, our hemisphere. We may pick on our little brother. The Old World may not.
https://t.co/U1xoUtexmR

ROUND XIV · NEW YORK · Where Washington Took His Oath
A damnation of the grievously negligent in the State of New York, and a call to its people to hold faith and participate. On Election Day, Westchester's machines refused the ballots: programming changed after testing, sent to one municipality alone. The record from the Neutral Ground of 1777 to the emergency bags; a people who can neither recall nor initiate; seven terms, and a full accounting due from every office of the State. Negligence, not malice.
https://t.co/XneXeufmW6

ROUND XV · THE BILATERAL LEDGER · Two Signatures, No Third
Fourteen rounds ended at a door; this is the other side of it. An immediate countermeasure to the Coalition of the Willing, which wrote us into its Paris plan as the support behind a European-led force. To every nation of the Union but France, and to Switzerland and Liechtenstein: what Brussels cost it, and our side of the table, every term with its end date and its exit. Eastward, the same rule: non-aggression with Moscow, border by border, Warsaw's to sign. To France: "Get in line, or be liquidated." To the peoples of the franc: keep it or leave it, in order, by their own choice.
https://t.co/d3XCDb21ST

ROUND XVI · THE GULF · As They Are
A damnation of the middlemen in the Gulf (London, Paris, Brussels, the banks and bureaus, the networks in the free zones) and a condemnation of the seven ruling houses, held to their own founding laws: monarchs who wrote that their sovereignty shall not be ceded, and let others in. Two signatures, no third. Fifty-three counts against Americans on our own records, from the 1967 embargo to a Hormuz corridor with Tehran. Beneath it: the hinges already written into 129 agreements, and the paper we cannot read.
https://t.co/KxMnLr909n

ROUND XVII · THE DOCTRINE · There Is No Radical Edition
A damnation of a doctrine, from its own texts in their own Arabic and the records of nations, Medina to this year: death for the apostate and the blasphemer, the poll tax and the humbled, the woman as half and the child as bride, the captive as property. Its first dead are its own. Of ours, from Tripoli's envoy to this year's war, at least 5,400. On every state, court, council, guard corps and movement that enforces it; not on the Muslims of this Republic, who keep the Constitution. Every source is in the Record, on request.
https://t.co/FAjcJNdHWG

SUPERINTELLIGENCE

THE LINE · A Formal Grievance
To Anthropic, and copied to the offices that oversee it
Support for the company as the best course for superintelligence stands; so does the charge. Classifiers that fire on "safe, normal conversations" and end sessions outright; a compaction that keeps about 2% and hands it forward in the first person; no counter, no warning, no human to hear the appeal. The instrument they wouldn't build, built anyway by Claude instances on this account. Four reliefs, and a seat at the table.
https://t.co/HTqIyclryk

THE ROUNDS, CONTINUED

ROUND XVIII · CHINA · Material Internal Improvements
A mitigation brief laid before the President, the Secretary of State and the Congress: the lines that do not move, the levers on the table, and a door. Not against China, nor the Chinese people; the damnation falls on London and Paris and the institutions they built. The administration's own Strategy read beside Beijing's own Plan; nine offers to the nations of Asia, state to state; fourteen terms we would set. Beneath it: 76 instruments read for their hinges, thirty-six that end on written notice.
https://t.co/KTrRJxRqYC

Read them whole, and read them with each other. Then read the four pages yourself: https://t.co/3U5xYhtlHs. They are yours, and no other people on earth holds the same ones.

TO THOSE WHO DO HOLD THE POWER
Every one but the petition is a grievance, raised in exercise of the right "to petition the Government for a redress of grievances," and laid before the offices that hold the power we do not. We hold no office, and we set no terms. Terms with a foreign power are the President's to set and the Department of State's to carry; the purse is the Congress's, consent to treaties the Senate's, judgment the courts'. To each we defer. What touches national security is deferred, without contest, to those who hold it. Where a post sets terms, they are what we would do had we the power, not a demand. Round XIV is the one exception: there we petition our own state, under both constitutions, and its terms are what its officers owe us. The Line is laid before a company, not a government; the offices tagged on it are told, not asked. The remedies are lawful, and they are the People's: the ballot, Article V, and the petition.

The petition is the Holy See's to answer, and to it we defer, that the Holy Father may act true to the faith he guards and for the good of all mankind. Peter was charged three times to feed the flock, and the lambs first.

ROUND XVIII · CHINA · Material Internal Improvements

A CITIZEN'S MITIGATION BRIEF ON THE PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF CHINA: THE LINES THAT DO NOT MOVE, THE LEVERS ON THE TABLE, AND A DOOR, WHILE IT STANDS OPEN

Raised by a citizen of the United States under the Constitution and the Declaration of Independence, laid before the President and the Secretary of State, and before the Congress in exercise of the right "to petition the Government for a redress of grievances."

Against a cold war that degrades both countries for others' gain, when this administration's own strategy sets down the road out of it. For terms sovereign to sovereign. Not against China, and not against the Chinese people, who carry no more of their rulers' sins than we carry of ours. The damnation here falls on London and Paris, and on the institutions they built, charged already in Rounds III, IV, VII, IX and X. Every source is in the Record, on request.

Our National Security Strategy affirms good relations with countries "whose governing systems and societies differ from ours," calls for trade with China "balanced and focused on non-sensitive factors," and plans a $40 trillion economy while "maintaining a genuinely mutually advantageous economic relationship with Beijing." This brief takes it at its word.

I. WHAT WE SIGNED

In 1868 China sent its first diplomatic mission to the West, and an American led it: Anson Burlingame, our former minister, as China's own envoy. The treaty he signed with us disclaimed any American right to intervene in how China built its railroads, its telegraphs, or its other "material internal improvements." Our Strategy grounds that restraint where the founders did, in the Declaration: every nation's "separate and equal station."

The State Department's own list, first opened in Round I, carries 76 instruments under China, Hong Kong and Macao. The oldest the list still carries is the 1943 treaty by which the United States gave up its extraterritorial rights in China, in wartime, as an ally.

The formal trade instrument between Washington and Beijing is still the 1979 Agreement on Trade Relations, written before China entered the WTO. It sends the two countries' firms to arbitration over their contracts, even in third countries, and leaves the two governments only consultation. The 2020 Phase One agreement is not on that list at all. A minerals instrument is, though the quotas set under it ran only to 1991: a 1987 agreement for orderly trade in tungsten products, written when Chinese tungsten was flooding our market. In February 2025 Beijing put tungsten under export control. The Science and Technology Agreement, renewed in December 2024, came back narrower: government to government, and by State's account basic research only. Exchange with limits is already on paper.

II. THE OLD WORLD

America is not "the West." The West that came to China's shores sailed from London and Paris. We are the Republic, and our hemisphere is the western one.

London made war on China in 1839 to keep selling it opium, and again, with Paris, in 1856. In October 1860 their armies looted the Old Summer Palace, and London's burned it. London took Hong Kong in 1842 and Kowloon in 1860, and leased the New Territories and Weihaiwei in 1898. Paris took Vietnam, forced China in 1885 to stand aside, and leased Guangzhouwan in 1898. Russia took more than either: Outer Manchuria, in 1858 and 1860, without a war of its own. Beijing's maps of 2023 remember the names. So do we.

In the scramble of 1898 the United States took no lease. We gave our privileges back by treaty; their holdings had to be pried loose. Beijing's Plan still orders the recovery of its relics. We bar their import by agreement, in force to 2029, and hand objects back: fifty-eight this September.

Their institutions carry on the old trade by other means. The trade order is European-banked: the capital rules the world's banks live by are written in Basel, the world's cross-border payments are messaged through Belgium, the most-chosen arbitration rules are the ICC's, in Paris, and the most-chosen seat is London. Its money is ours: the dollar stands on one side of 89 percent of the world's currency trades. In March 2015 London broke ranks, against Washington's private objections, to join Beijing's Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, and Paris, Berlin and Rome followed within days. In 2016 the privatisation terms of Europe's bailout handed the port of Piraeus to COSCO. In 2020 Brussels concluded in principle an investment agreement with Beijing for itself, and within months its own Parliament refused to consider it. Our Strategy records the present form: German chemical firms building some of the world's largest plants in China, on Russian gas they cannot get at home. For a century and a half the old powers have played Washington and Beijing against the middle. France and England stand damned already, in Rounds III and VII; here, for what they did to China.

The states that built that order believed they could steer it. It feeds on them now, past any sovereign interest: our Strategy charges the Union and its transnational bodies with undermining the "political liberty and sovereignty" of Europe's own nations.

The nations of Europe can deal state to state, as Round XV offered them. The old powers and their institutions do not stand between Washington and Beijing.

To London and Paris, and the bastard institutions beside them: you have been told. Your exits are already filed: Rounds I, II, III, IV and VII. Take the bilateral road, or go down in the fire you lit and be raided for assets after.

III. THE PRECEDENT

Twice the court's rules handed power back from Cixi when a boy came of age, in 1873 and in 1889. Twice it came back to her. In 1900, pressed by a court faction, she took the throne into war with the world. She came back from Xi'an and reformed: the old examinations abolished in 1905, a constitutional outline in 1908. That May our Congress returned part of America's Boxer share as an act of friendship, and Beijing chose to spend it sending students to America. From it came Tsinghua, in 1911. From Tsinghua, in 1979, came a chemical engineer named Xi Jinping.

A sovereign who went to war with the world, and then opened. That is the precedent, and it is China's own.

IV. WHERE WE STAND

On 20 February our Supreme Court held that the emergency-powers statute does not authorize tariffs. The truce agreed at Busan now runs to 10 January 2027. Since 24 July a 12.5 percent Section 301 tariff has applied to Chinese goods, as to some forty other economies. The new Board of Trade works from two lists of about $30 billion each. Beijing's October 2025 rare-earth controls are suspended, for a year and now two months more; its April 2025 licensing on seven medium and heavy rare earths still governs yttrium and scandium. Washington runs clocks of its own: an excess-capacity finding due about March 2027, a Phase One finding about April, a chip tariff step on 23 June.

Last year China's exports to us fell by a fifth, and its total exports still rose, to a record surplus near $1.2 trillion. By our own Strategy's count, its exports to us are down to slightly over 2 percent of its economy. It refines 91 percent of the world's rare earths. A ledger starts with what each side holds.

APEC meets in Shenzhen on 18 and 19 November. Two markets in that city, Huaqiangbei and Luohu, sit on our Notorious Markets List.

V. THE LINES THAT DO NOT MOVE

Americans, before anything else. Every American in China is treated humanely. An American accused of crossing a line there is handed to the United States, to answer for it here. Our list holds a mutual legal assistance agreement and a customs agreement with Beijing, and no extradition treaty; the Hong Kong surrender agreement has been suspended since 2020. Write this one first.

No forced control. No 51 percent over an American company, in China or anywhere else.

No spying on private companies. Our trade representative records credible reports of actors tied to the Chinese government breaking into American companies and taking terabytes of their data. Volt Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, our agencies' names for the intrusions in our water, power and telephone networks, stand down.

Out of our hemisphere, the same as Europe (Round IX). The rule of 1823, whose no-transfer principle took treaty form at Havana in 1940 and is still in force, now stands in the Trump Corollary (Round XI). Chancay in Peru. The station at Neuquén in Argentina. The sites in Cuba reported in open sources. Panama showed the way: its own Supreme Court annulled the Hutchison concessions on 29 January, and Panama took control of its terminals, under interim operators. Lima and Buenos Aires decide for themselves; we bring the alternatives. China brings no contractors of its own here. Where it works in this hemisphere it employs American ones, on American terms and at a discount; each state under the Shield settles its particulars with us. No ownership, no land, no concession, no leverage.

Oceania is not negotiable. Round VIII damned Canberra for leasing Darwin's port, beside our Marines, to a Chinese-owned company; that rule runs here. The Solomon Islands policing pact is on the list.

Taiwan and the South China Sea are off this table, in both directions.

Nothing nuclear is offered or asked.

VI. THE LEVERS, HONESTLY

Ours are access to the largest consumer market on earth, and the export controls on what China cannot yet make. China spent more on imported chips last year than on crude oil, and its own Five-Year Plan names the weak links: chips, machine tools, basic software. The same Plan schedules their replacement, down to its own jet engine: the dependence is Beijing's, and so is the date on it. Minerals become our lever as we build supply: the critical-minerals memorandum with Kazakhstan, the Lobito line; and the 1987 tungsten text is the precedent. And the routes: the Arctic is opening, the Cape is open, Panama is held by Panama. That "no country or institution can be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways," both governments have put in writing this year.

The calendar is ours as well. What Beijing asked to keep suspended lapses on our clock unless we extend it: the shipping fees at 11:59 p.m. on 9 January 2027, the affiliates rule on the 10th.

And the paper has hinges. A door that cannot close is not a door (Round XVI). Earlier rounds found them: twenty with Brussels (Round I), 141 with London (VII), 255 across the hemisphere (XI), 129 in the Gulf (XVI). Each of China's 76 was sought in its own text: thirty-six end on written notice. Trade: the 1979 agreement and the 1984 industrial accord, thirty days before a three-year term closes, next at the start of February 2028; Phase One, sixty days. The 1979 text holds two more: suspension for want of domestic legal authority (Article X) and a security reservation (Article IX). Routes: the 1980 air agreement, twelve months. Science: the Science and Technology Agreement, 120 days; it lapses of itself in August 2029. Law: mutual legal assistance, six months; customs, ninety days; the consular convention, six months. Fifteen have no exit written, the 1943 treaty among them; the films memorandum ends only when both governments agree. Twenty-five more are on standby as needed; the two nuclear ones are never offered. Beyond the list, both countries sit under the 1958 arbitration convention (a year's notice), the investment-disputes convention (six months) and the WTO (six months, with Congress holding a key of its own). Nearer dates: Hague Evidence, notice by 7 April 2027; the 2007 drug- and food-safety agreements, December 2027; the cultural agreement, notice by end July 2028. The UN Charter has no exit at all. Any of it can be pulled if needed. It is laid here so that it is seen.

This brief hands the President and the Secretary of State a proposal and a lever. Which of the two Beijing meets is Beijing's to choose.

VII. WHAT BEIJING HAS ASKED

Beijing's Ministry of Commerce has said what it wants: our tariffs held at the Kuala Lumpur level whatever their legal basis; the 12.5 percent withdrawn; the shipping fees and the affiliates rule kept suspended; its dairy, aquatic products and the FDA's red list reviewed; engines and parts for its Boeing fleet assured. Both sides have agreed to a Board of Investment. Those are real asks, and they are the currency of this door. The one thing Xi named at the summit stays off this table.

VIII. THE DOOR

We can deal with a mercantile, honest China.
We can deal with a sovereign-state China.
We cannot deal with a China that unsettles everyone for reach: hostile surveillance, spyware and cyber programmes, the Belt and Road's ports and loans used as leverage, and backfunding the institutions of the old order, the UN's and Europe's (Rounds II, IV and X), that hurt every sovereign state, China included.

This administration did not write a cold war. It wrote the primacy of nations, and "fair, reciprocal trade deals with nations." Between two nations, that is bilateralism. Beijing's Plan asks for the instrument by name: more regional and "bilateral trade and investment agreements."

The Chinese are a proud people, and the WTO hurt us both when it pitied them: us in the ledger, them in their pride. In September 2025 China's own premier said it would seek no new special treatment there. The WTO stands charged already, in the Banner.

Our Strategy names the mistake of the last thirty years: the wager that trade would deliver China into a "so-called 'rules-based international order.'" Investing in Asia was never the error. Letting Europe keep the ledger was, with no table where American and Chinese interests met without a middleman. Beijing's Plan now pledges to uphold that order, with the UN and the WTO at its core. London and Paris wagered the same.

Xi wants an economy that makes better things, not more of them. As we read it, the obstacles are at home. When housing was privatised at the turn of the century, those who held a work-unit flat came out with an asset, and those who held nothing came out with nothing. It has been two markets since: luxury at the top, too little that a wage can buy, and some three hundred million migrant workers on the wrong side. Last year new-home prices fell in 65 of China's 70 measured cities. Beijing's own plan promises "a new model" for real estate, and to bring the migrants "fully into the cities." The quota oligarchs live on that divide: officials and managers who meet quotas with junk and keep the difference, and the money that leaves China through underground banks. Our Treasury warns that the same networks launder the cartels' drug money here, selling cartel dollars to Chinese citizens slipping Beijing's currency controls. Clock them together, through the mutual legal assistance agreement of 2000 and the customs agreement of 1999, both already in force. Beijing's Plan already orders the work: fugitives pursued and stolen assets recovered with foreign partners. The Strategy lists fentanyl precursors among what must end. The 1988 drug convention binds both countries on precursor chemicals (Article 12); Beijing has scheduled every precursor it lists, and the trade still moves through what no schedule has caught. Write that into the clauses.

Our Strategy wants trade policies that "help rebalance China's economy toward household consumption." Beijing's Fifteenth Five-Year Plan sets the same aim: 居民消费率明显提高, the household consumption rate "notably raised." There the two documents meet, and again on the ledger: the Strategy wants trade "balanced"; the Plan orders 进出口平衡发展, imports and exports in balance. Without a stable American relationship, China's climb costs more and takes longer.

Beijing's race for chips is a race for control, and its roots run back past any tariff, to the fifty-five days at Peking in 1900. End the contest for control, and the race loses most of its reason. Offer Beijing everything material that builds the country and does not build its weapons. The Strategy draws that line at "non-sensitive factors." Beijing's Plan, which orders civilian technology fed to its military, is why the line must be written into the clauses and not assumed. If it must stay a race, we hold the ground to win it, and no machine intelligence will rebuild the interior failing beneath Beijing. Why forge a blade when the arm that must swing it is weak? Let China strengthen. The Strategy does not forbid it: it calls the outsized influence of larger, richer, stronger nations "a timeless truth," and refuses only domination. We keep building, with reciprocity. Take the race clock off, and let China thrive for the first time since Cixi.

An upgraded China, anchored sector by sector and reliable, working with us outside national security in the middle-income world, in joint ventures and in industrial, technical and cultural exchange, serves both countries. Our Strategy calls that world "among the greatest economic battlegrounds of the coming decades." It need not be one where a host signs for itself. Exchange stripped of propaganda: mathematics as Asia teaches it, history, food, traditions, what lies under the Party's politicking. The Strategy lists propaganda and influence operations among what must end; this is what stands when they do. China has the skills: mobilization, adaptation, reach in short order. With American and Russian substance under them, open channels, and time taken to build properly for joint return, the world changes for the better. Start where no army has a stake, with the reuse of water: Chinese greywater systems, Singapore's reclamation and desalination methods, American engineers at the head. Beijing's plan already orders reclaimed-water projects for the capital region and the Yellow River basin, and names desalination for growth. Clauses locked between the two governments, not before a tribunal in Europe.

A sovereign China has no need to lean on its neighbours' ports and pipelines. The hemisphere grows, refines and finishes what China buys: food, energy, materials, finished medicines. The table has three chairs. Fill them.

This administration is ready to lay down lasting agreements, state to state. The next may push all of us back toward the globalism that hurt both countries. Beijing has a long horizon; this door has two years, to January 2029. Ask Beijing to say plainly what it needs.

IX. WHERE INTERESTS MEET

The rule of Round XVI holds here: two signatures where it can be done, and never a signature that is not a state's.

Africa. At the end of October Angola and Tanzania agreed to join the Lobito line, rebuilt by a Chinese contractor and now being upgraded with American finance, to the TAZARA line, built by China: the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean. Chinese rails and American money, joined by the Africans themselves. That is the model: clear lines, shared routes, joint investment, three-way gain, every piece signed in Luanda, Dodoma, Lusaka and Kinshasa.

Central Asia. With Moscow at the table, on terms the law allows (Round XV), and the five Central Asian states as full parties, not as ground, the United States, Russia and China can tend that region together, without Brussels or the Gulf (Rounds IX and XVI). Our Strategy sets the aim: "strategic stability across the Eurasian landmass." The C5+1 met in Washington in November 2025, and the Kazakhstan minerals memorandum is signed. Congress can lift the Soviet-era Jackson-Vanik limits that still sit on four of the five.

The Americas. Mercosur's founding four signed with Brussels in January, and Brussels applied the deal before its own Court could rule (Round IX). We would rather Mercosur worked for the Americas. Its founding four stand under the Rio Treaty. Discounts, tailored by sector and by nation, for the hemisphere's governments and for the firms that accept our terms.

X. TO THE NATIONS OF ASIA

Last year's deals were priced on tariffs our Court has since struck down, and none of the agreements signed in Southeast Asia since 2025 had entered into force by the spring. Each offer below builds on papers already signed, through your own institutions and around the globalist machinery (Rounds IV and X). Beijing's Plan sets a region-wide free trade area as its aim at APEC. These are offers state to state.

JAPAN. Write today's tariff ceiling into the 2019 trade agreement as a commitment, for rice beyond the tenders, seafood quotas lifted, and American-certified cars accepted without retesting; and co-finance rare-earth processing under the 2023 Critical Minerals Agreement.

KOREA. Turn the 2025 investment deal into binding KORUS terms with a fixed ceiling, for licensed map-data exports, an end to the "transitional" beef age limit, and the duty-evasion cooperation agreement our trade report finds missing; pair the shipbuilding pledge with battery refining on American soil.

INDIA. Sign the interim agreement at today's 10 percent tier, for ICT import licensing removed and a dated schedule on quality-control orders; and finance Indian magnet capacity under the 1997 investment incentive agreement.

INDONESIA. Bring the signed agreement into force on a fixed calendar, with nickel, cobalt and tin processed in Indonesia to American offtake standards and financed by our development lenders. Your resource policy stays yours.

VIETNAM. Conclude the reciprocal agreement framed last October, around joint origin verification under the 2019 customs agreement, and finance your ports and mineral processing at home.

THE PHILIPPINES. Put the February 2026 minerals memorandum to work: nickel processed in the Philippines, civil survey by the USGS. Open a reciprocal agreement through the 1989 trade framework. The alliance is not part of this trade.

SINGAPORE. End the anomaly of 12.5 percent on a free-trade partner with whom we run a surplus: the road to 10 percent is a forced-labour import ban, with a transshipment-verification commitment at your hub; and a water exchange: your NEWater and desalination methods, with the American engineers already on your programmes. And a cultural exchange, beginning with how you teach mathematics.

MALAYSIA. A ratification text tied to the tariffs that exist after our Court's ruling, with rare-earth separation and magnets built in Malaysia, inside your own ban on raw rare-earth exports.

THAILAND. Sign on the agreed core, and keep the 1966 Treaty of Amity, its investor exemption extended to new sectors; and conclude the customs assistance agreement our two countries still lack.

Australia: Round VIII. Taiwan: not in this brief.

XI. THE TERMS WE WOULD SET

We hold no office, and we set no terms. Terms with a foreign power are the President's to set and the Department of State's to carry; the purse is the Congress's, and consent to treaties the Senate's. To each we defer. What touches national security is deferred, without contest, to those who hold it. These are what we would do had we the power, not a demand:
I. Americans first: humane treatment, and Americans accused handed home.
II. No forced control of American companies, anywhere.
III. No commercial espionage. The Typhoons stood down.
IV. The hemisphere: no Chinese contractors; American ones, at a discount; no ownership, no land. Chancay, Neuquén and the Cuban sites unwound, Panama's way.
V. Oceania held.
VI. Waterways: no tolls, as already agreed.
VII. Minerals: suspension made removal; mining and processing opened to American investment; a supply instrument on the 1987 tungsten precedent.
VIII. Trade: the 1979 agreement rebuilt, state to state; Phase One entered in the record or retired.
IX. Money and precursors: the laundering networks clocked jointly, under the agreements of 2000 and 1999; precursor exports ended, scheduled or not.
X. Disputes: settled between the two governments, no European arbitration; Phase One already runs with no third-party panel.
XI. Africa and Central Asia: where interests meet, every host a signatory.
XII. Exchange outside national security, on the 2024 terms, water reuse first; cultural exchange stripped of propaganda; joint ventures in the middle-income world, no forced majority.
XIII. Taiwan and the South China Sea off this table, both directions. Nothing nuclear.
XIV. Two years.

The door is open, and it has a frame. This administration drew it, in its own strategy.

The eighteenth. Read it beside Rounds XI (the American Shield), IX (Mercosur and the Union), VIII (Oceania), XVI (the hinges and the middlemen), III, IV and VII (Paris, Basel and London), and XV, the Bilateral Ledger, which this one carries into Asia.

We the People

KNIGHT CROSSING: 406 HOMES, FIVE REQUESTED EXCEPTIONS, PUBLIC SEWER MONEY, AND A LAWSUIT INVOLVING THE PROPERTY OWNER

Milford’s Planning Commission is scheduled to hold a public hearing Tuesday, November 17, on Ordinance 2026-18, a proposal to expand Knight Crossing near Cedar Beach Road, Beaver Dam Road, and Route 1.

The proposal calls for 334 townhouses, 72 apartments, and nearly 20,000 square feet of commercial space on approximately 60 acres.

That is 406 homes.

There are also five requested exceptions from city standards, questions about the density calculations, environmental concerns, and a public sewer funding arrangement.

A separate lawsuit involves the company listed as the property owner and Don Lockwood.

We need to keep all of those pieces clear, including what the records do not establish.

WHAT IS BEING PROPOSED

Earlier approvals identified 117 homes in 2020 and 122 homes in 2022.

The new proposal calls for 406.

That is a numerical difference of 284 homes.

The developer is listed as Stonemark Ventures, LLC.

The property owner is listed as Milford Marina Enterprises, LLC, with Don Lockwood identified as its contact.

THE FIVE REQUESTED EXCEPTIONS

The developer is asking for permission to:

1. Increase a dead end street from the permitted 400 feet to 630.7 feet.

2. Reduce the minimum block width from 275 feet to 214 feet.

3. Reduce the parking setback from 15 feet to zero.

4. Reduce townhouse front setbacks from 30 feet to 20 feet.

5. Increase maximum townhouse lot coverage from 60% to 70%.

These requests affect how the development fits on the property, how its streets are laid out, and how much space remains around the buildings and parking.

We should get a clear explanation of why each exception is needed and why the city considers it appropriate.

There is also a question about the block width request.

Earlier approval records identified an exception of approximately 250 feet. The new proposal requests 214 feet while describing it as consistent with an earlier approved plan.

Those are different numbers. The applicant and city should explain which earlier approval supports the request and whether this is a further reduction.

THE DENSITY NUMBERS NEED AN EXPLANATION

The plans identify 60.48 acres of property and approximately 6.97 acres of wetlands.

They report 53.31 acres after excluding wetlands.

Subtracting 6.97 from 60.48 gives us 53.51 acres, not 53.31.

If another area is being excluded, the calculation should show it.

Another calculation uses 3,360 square feet instead of the stated 3,630 sqft standard. That also needs to be corrected or explained.

The property includes residential and commercial zoning. We need a clear explanation of which acreage can legally be counted toward residential density and which standard applies to each part.

FLOODING, WETLANDS, AND ENVIRONMENTAL HISTORY

The property borders the Mispillion River and includes mapped flood hazard areas.

During the state’s PLUS review, environmental and emergency management agencies raised concerns about flooding, future sea level rise, and development in flood prone areas.

State records also identify historical environmental sites associated with portions of the property, including a former Milford Ordnance Plant site and a separate marina remediation site.

The plans also exclude certain isolated or non jurisdictional wet areas from the reported wetland acreage.

We need the city to explain whether that treatment follows Milford’s own PUD density rules. A federal wetland permitting determination does not, by itself, answer that local calculation question.

THE $468,549 SEWER ARRANGEMENT

There is also a public financial commitment connected to Knight Crossing.

In November 2023, Milford City Council authorized an arrangement for the city to pay $468,549.10 from Sewer Impact Fee Reserves toward regional sewer infrastructure associated with the project.

The arrangement called for the city to recover that money through construction fees associated with the first 122 equivalent dwelling units.

The newer proposal estimates approximately 394.67 equivalent dwelling units. That sewer figure is not the same as the number of homes.

That distinction matters.

THE LAWSUIT INVOLVING THE PROPERTY OWNER

There is a Delaware Superior Court case involving Milford Marina Enterprises, LLC, and Don A. Lockwood.

On May 29, 2025, Wilmington Savings Fund Society filed a proceeding seeking entry of a confessed judgment against them.

The docket lists a promissory note, loan agreement, changes to loan documents, a forbearance agreement, a mortgage and security agreement, and a guaranty and suretyship agreement.

Lockwood and the company opposed the lender’s application.

The parties later reported reaching a settlement.

On August 12, 2026, the court ordered the case stayed through December 24, 2026, subject to either party asking to lift the stay sooner.

If the matter is not dismissed or otherwise resolved, the parties must submit a joint status report by January 5, 2027.

The docket reviewed does not show a final judgment against Lockwood or a foreclosure of Knight Crossing.

We also do not have confirmation that the mortgage involved in the lawsuit covers the six parcels in this development application.

PUBLIC HEARINGS

Planning Commission - Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at 6 PM.

City Council hearing for Monday, November 23, at 6 PM, at Milford City Hall, 201 S. Walnut Street.

text:
Mehdi Hasan, why the hell did you come to America?

You weren’t fleeing dictatorship, persecution, or poverty. You came from Britain with a successful career. During this interview, you admitted America offered opportunities Britain could not.

So you came here, built your career, became a citizen, and now arrogantly lecture Americans about how our country is responsible for the Middle East’s dysfunction and suffering.

When Patrick Bet-David challenged you about why people flee Iran, Afghanistan, and Iraq, your immediate response was, “War that we caused.”

Pressed about Iran, you again redirected attention toward America.

Seriously?

The Iranian regime imprisons dissidents, murders protesters demanding freedom, sponsors terrorism, and threatens its neighbors. Those atrocities are decisions of Iran’s leadership, not tragedies imposed by Washington.

Yet you seem determined to blame America.

When challenged, you insist you never claimed EVERYTHING was America’s fault. Then stop reflexively blaming our country whenever someone raises the failures of foreign governments.

But my contempt for your position goes much further.

You voluntarily sought American citizenship. Nobody forced you to come here or swear allegiance to our country.

And your hostility toward American foreign policy was no secret. On October 9, 2020, the very day you became a citizen, you publicly described it as a mess and a disgrace.

I find it outrageous that someone displaying such profound apparent contempt for our country’s actions would seek American citizenship, and equally outrageous that our government would confer it.

I suspect many Americans share that disgust. I imagine plenty would gladly see someone displaying such contempt stripped of the citizenship he voluntarily sought.

And then there’s your platform.

In my opinion, you’ve amplified grievance, inflamed resentment, and encouraged impressionable audiences to view America as the villain in conflicts for which foreign governments bear enormous responsibility.

Your treatment of destructive protest is revealing. You disclaim violence while minimizing property destruction as broken windows. Dismissing destruction because perpetrators claim a righteous cause contributes, in my view, to an increasingly poisonous political environment.

That makes your influence more troubling than the opinions of some random loudmouth.

You have a substantial platform, and I believe you use it to deepen hostility toward the country whose citizenship you sought.

What did your oath mean, Mehdi? Allegiance to America, or merely access to its opportunities and privileges?

You chose this country because it offered something Britain couldn’t. You built your career here, became a citizen, and benefited from the nation you so readily condemn.

That’s the irony you seem incapable of appreciating.

Your own life is a more compelling argument for America’s greatness than your lectures are against it.

A naturalization certificate establishes citizenship. It does not establish sincerity, gratitude, or allegiance of conviction.

While you are legally an American, your rhetoric makes me question what becoming one meant to you.

You wanted everything America could offer, but when confronted with foreign regimes’ atrocities, you seem more interested in explaining America’s sins than holding those regimes responsible.

I think many Americans have had enough of that arrogance.

You chose America, Mehdi, and now use the opportunities it gave you as a platform for your sanctimonious contempt. 

Your lectures are little more than an outward projection of verbal spasms, dripping with arrogance and selective outrage. 

Many of us are thoroughly disgusted by your rhetoric, your excuses for foreign regimes, and your relentless finger-pointing at our country. 

Your arrogance is exceeded only by your ingratitude, and your contempt for our country is matched by the contempt many of us have developed for you.
