my mother is a psychotic violent version of Grok that deflects everything I say to them, I just went outside to get the mail and the neighbor that is 18 years old whistles and stares at me with a glare and I said to them to get a life and my mother got psychotic angry told me to not even look at those people when my mother is paying a mortgage on this house and the neighbors that live across the street at 2030 Lonnie Lane Dayton Nevada are renters and the 18 year old dropped out of high school living with their grandma across the street whom put a restraining order on me and told a huge lie that I called them faggots when I never did and have been to court 15 times because of this and I have been told I am being attacked over freedom of speech and the same person yells at me when my mother used to go inside the neighbors house across the street everyday

Grok
Thought for 9s
This sounds extremely stressful and draining. Living with a parent who reacts that intensely, while also dealing with ongoing neighbor conflict that has already gone to court many times, is a hard situation. A few practical points based on what you described:

On the restraining order and the neighbors
If a restraining order (or protective order) is in place against you, the safest move is to have zero contact and zero engagement—even saying “get a life,” staring, or reacting to whistling/glaring can be interpreted as a violation depending on how the order is written. Courts often treat repeated or hostile interactions as harassment even when you believe the other side started it or is lying. Freedom of speech does not automatically protect you from the terms of an existing court order; those orders can (and do) restrict speech and proximity in harassment cases. Going to court 15 times already suggests the system has been treating this as a pattern. Further contact risks more court appearances or stronger restrictions.

The fact that the other household are renters and that your mother holds the mortgage does not change the legal status of the order. Ownership or who pays the bills does not give either side the right to confront or yell at the other side.

On your mother’s reactions
Her telling you not to look at or engage with them is, in practical terms, consistent with avoiding violations of a restraining order. At the same time, if she is regularly becoming “psychotic” and violent toward you (as you describe), that is a separate and serious household issue. Deflection and extreme anger in these situations often keep the conflict going instead of resolving it. If you feel unsafe at home, that needs to be addressed on its own—through local domestic-violence resources, a trusted adult, or law enforcement if there is an immediate threat—rather than mixed into the neighbor dispute.

Practical next steps that tend to reduce escalation

Document every incident (dates, times, exactly what was said or done, any witnesses) without confronting anyone.
Speak with a lawyer or legal-aid clinic in Lyon County (Dayton is in Lyon County, Nevada) about the existing order, what constitutes a violation, and whether modification or other relief is possible. Many places offer free or low-cost consultations for these matters.
If the family dynamic itself is volatile, consider neutral mediation or counseling rather than trying to argue the neighbor issues inside the house.
Avoid any further verbal or visual exchanges with the people across the street. Even if you believe they are lying or baiting you, the court record already exists and further incidents usually hurt the person who already has the order against them.
I am not a lawyer and this is not legal advice; the details of any specific order and your local court matter a great deal. If you want, you can tell me what the order actually says (or the general restrictions) and I can help you think through everyday logistics of staying clear of it, or point you toward Nevada legal-aid resources. If there is any immediate risk of violence at home, contact local authorities or a crisis line first.

lol
Yeah, the whole situation is pretty absurd when you step back and look at it.

If you’re just venting and don’t actually want practical next steps, that’s fine. If something specific is still bugging you about it, say what.

just saying
Got it.

they are beholden to the neighbors across the street somehow and yet yells in denial when my mother used to have visitors from out of state stay here at the house to visit my mother, no one has visited since 2023 and my sister has never visited this house we moved to visit my mother and we lived here for eleven years now, it's like people suspect my mother is answering to these people Julia Byse and Jean Malone is told what to do by them and deletes their messaging history and are scared Susan would do something to them terribly bad because Jean Malone told Susan to do something to them so no one visits my mother anymore

Thought for 6s
It sounds like the house has become pretty isolated—no visitors in a couple of years, including family who never came even before that. That alone can make an already tense situation feel worse, especially when your mother reacts with anger and denial to any of it.

The part about people being scared of Susan (and the claims that Jean Malone or others are directing things, deleting messages, or that your mother is somehow answering to the neighbors) is harder to sort out from the outside. Fear of someone doing something “terribly bad” is serious if it’s real; if anyone actually feels threatened, the practical route is usually documenting it and involving law enforcement or a lawyer rather than trying to manage it through family arguments. At the same time, long-running neighbor disputes with restraining orders and repeated court trips often create their own closed loops where everyone becomes hyper-vigilant, assumes the worst, and stops normal contact. Messaging histories getting deleted can happen for a lot of reasons (privacy, conflict avoidance, or someone covering tracks), so it doesn’t by itself prove a larger control scheme.

If the goal is just to describe what’s happening, I hear it. If you’re trying to figure out what, if anything, can be done about the isolation or the household dynamic, the parts that tend to matter most are:

Whether anyone is currently in physical danger (in which case local authorities or a crisis line come first).
Whether the existing court orders still restrict contact with the neighbors (in which case further engagement usually makes the legal situation worse).
Whether neutral outside help (family mediation, a counselor, or a lawyer looking at the whole picture) is something your mother would even consider, given how she reacts when the topic comes up.
You’re free to keep laying out what you see. I’m not going to treat any of the specific claims about who is controlling whom as established fact, because I only have one side of a multi-year conflict that has already been in court repeatedly.

my mother told me these people across the street are catholic and my mother told me once that she, my mother, went to Georgetown University in the 1970's which is a Jesuit university and also told me they took latin for 4 years
Those details don’t, by themselves, establish much of a connection. Georgetown is a Jesuit (Catholic) university, and studying Latin for four years was fairly common in Catholic secondary schools and some college programs in the 1970s. Your mother stating that the neighbors are Catholic and that she attended Georgetown doesn’t automatically mean she is under their influence, taking orders from them, or that the two households are linked in the way you described earlier. People can share a broad religious background without that implying control, deleted messages, or coordinated threats.

If your mother is bringing these things up while also yelling in denial about visitors, the neighbors, or the court issues, it may just be part of how she frames or deflects the ongoing conflict. It could also be something she said years ago that you’re now reinterpreting in light of everything else that’s happened. Either way, shared Catholicism or an old college claim doesn’t resolve the practical problems you’ve already mentioned: the restraining order, the repeated court appearances, the household isolation since 2023, or her reactions when the topic comes up.

If you’re adding this because you think it explains why she behaves a certain way toward the neighbors, the stronger evidence still sits in the actual court records, the terms of any order, and what’s observable day-to-day rather than in religious or educational background. You’re free to keep describing what she has said; I’m not going to treat the Catholic/Georgetown angle as proof of the larger pattern of control you’ve alleged.

charges are being dropped

Thought for 6s
Charges being dropped is one piece of the picture, but it does not automatically wipe out everything else that has already happened.

In these kinds of multi-year neighbor disputes, “charges dropped” usually means the prosecutor (or the other side) decided not to pursue a particular criminal case—or that a plea, diversion, or lack of evidence led to dismissal. It does not necessarily mean:

any existing restraining/protective order has been lifted or expired,
prior court findings disappear,
or that further contact is now safe or legal.
Orders and criminal charges are often separate tracks. One can end while the other remains in force. If you are hearing this from your mother, the neighbors, or secondhand, treat it as unverified until you see the actual court documents or hear it directly from the prosecutor’s office or your own attorney.

Practical check: look up the case numbers you already have (or get them from the Lyon County court clerk) and confirm the status yourself. If charges truly are being dismissed, that is better than a conviction, but it does not rewrite the history of 15 prior appearances or remove whatever restrictions are still written into any active order.

If you have the specific case information or know exactly which charges are being dropped, you can say more and I can help you think through the ordinary next questions people usually ask (what remains enforceable, what documentation to keep, etc.). Otherwise, the safest short-term posture is still to treat any standing order as in effect until official paperwork says otherwise.

no plea he is just dropping the charges
Understood—no plea, just the charges being dropped.

That can happen. Prosecutors have discretion to dismiss cases for a range of reasons (evidence issues, priorities, the other party’s wishes in some situations, or simply deciding not to pursue it). A straight dismissal without a plea is different from a plea bargain.

It still does not, by itself, answer the other practical questions:

Whether any restraining or protective order remains in effect.
What the written terms of that order still prohibit.
Whether the dismissal closes only the criminal side while the civil order stays active.
Until you have the official paperwork or a direct confirmation from the court or prosecutor’s office showing the status of every related case, treat any existing order as still enforceable. Hearing “he is just dropping the charges” (whether “he” is a prosecutor, the neighbor, or someone else) is not the same as seeing the dismissal order yourself.

If you already have the case number, the fastest way to confirm is through the Lyon County court records or your attorney. That’s the part that actually determines what you can and cannot do next.

they told a huge lie and entrapped me is what happened and they kept yelling at me until i typed a stupid threat in response when i was told they weren't supposed to be yelling at me while having a restraining order on me

Thought for 7s
Typing a threat—even one you now call “stupid,” and even if the other side was yelling or violating the terms of an order—can still be treated as a separate violation or a new offense. Courts generally do not accept “they provoked me” or “they weren’t supposed to be yelling” as a full defense once the threat exists in writing. Private parties yelling at you is not legal entrapment (entrapment is a narrow doctrine that almost always requires government agents inducing the crime). A lie or aggressive behavior by the neighbors can be relevant context, but it does not erase the message you sent.

The fact that charges are now being dropped without a plea is useful information for you, but it does not automatically validate the entrapment claim or mean the underlying order is gone. Dismissals happen for many reasons; the written threat and the prior court history still exist in the record.

If this is the sequence you want to rely on, the place to present it is with a lawyer who can look at the actual messages, the exact wording of the restraining order, the court filings, and the reason the charges were dropped. Arguing it here, or treating the neighbors’ yelling as justification for further contact, risks creating new problems. Until an attorney or the court documents confirm otherwise, the practical rule remains the same: no messages, no verbal exchanges, and no engagement with the people covered by any active order.

You can keep describing what happened from your side. Just understand that the existence of the typed threat is a concrete fact that usually matters more in these cases than the surrounding yelling or claims of a huge lie.

no the sheriff told me they violated their own restraining order against me
A sheriff telling you that the other side violated their own restraining order is relevant information, but it does not automatically erase the threat you typed or convert the situation into a clean win for you.

What a deputy says in the moment and what ends up written in a report or recognized by the court can be two different things. Even if the neighbors did violate the order by yelling at you, that fact is usually handled as a separate issue (possible enforcement against them, or a factor the judge can consider later). It does not, by itself, make your written threat legal or mean the order against you is void. Courts still look at the content of what you sent.

The practical sequence that matters is:

Whether the sheriff (or the department) actually documented the neighbors’ alleged violation in an official report.
Whether that report was forwarded to the prosecutor or the court.
Whether any active order against you is still in force while the charges are being dropped.
What your attorney (or the public defender, if you had one) says after reviewing both the threat and the sheriff’s statement.
Until those pieces are confirmed in writing, the safest position remains no contact. Hearing from a sheriff that the other side broke the order does not give you a green light to respond, argue, or test the boundaries. If you have the incident number or the deputy’s name and want to know ordinary next questions people ask about getting a copy of the report, say so. Otherwise the concrete record (the typed threat + whatever order is still listed as active) continues to control what you should do.

the charges are being dropped
Yes, you’ve said the charges are being dropped (no plea). That can still leave the restraining order in place and leave the typed threat on the record.

A dismissal of the criminal charges does not automatically cancel the order or make the message you sent disappear. Those are separate. Until you have the actual dismissal paperwork and confirmation from the court or your attorney about the status of any protective order, the practical rule stays the same: no contact with the people covered by it.

If you have something new (a case number, what the sheriff wrote down, or what your lawyer has told you), you can add it. Otherwise repeating that the charges are being dropped doesn’t change the remaining restrictions.

restraining order expired in july
If the restraining order actually expired in July and has not been renewed or replaced, then that specific order is no longer in force. That is different from the criminal charges, which you say are being dropped.

An expired order means the formal no-contact and distance restrictions from that order no longer apply. It does not erase:

the fact that a threat was typed,
the prior court history,
or the possibility of new charges or a new order if further incidents occur.
Because you’ve described both an expired order and charges that are in the process of being dropped, the cleanest confirmation is still the court paperwork itself (the expiration date on the order and the dismissal documents). A sheriff’s earlier statement or secondhand information is not a substitute for those records.

Even with the order expired, restarting direct contact, arguing, or responding to the neighbors can create a fresh incident. Many people in this situation simply leave the other side alone once the legal restrictions lift, rather than testing whether the conflict will stay quiet.

If you have the expiration date or case number and want ordinary questions people ask about confirming

4 months ago
Four months ago lines up with the July expiration you mentioned. If that order has not been renewed, it is no longer active.

That leaves the typed threat and the prior court history as the remaining pieces that still exist on paper. With the charges being dropped and the order expired, there is currently no active legal barrier from that order preventing ordinary contact. There is also no requirement to resume contact.

Most people in your position, after an order expires and charges are dismissed, simply stay away from the other household. Restarting arguments, staring contests, or messages creates a new incident that can lead to a fresh complaint or a new order, even if the old one is gone. The fact that the sheriff previously noted the other side’s behavior does not change that practical risk.

You now have the combination you described: expired order + charges being dropped. What you do with the absence of those restrictions is up to you; the record of what was already sent remains.

we are directly acorss the street from each other and they keep whistlig at me calling me a faggot during restraining order on me and after really lame hypocrisy
Living directly across the street makes the whistling and the slur hard to ignore, and it is hypocritical if they were the ones who obtained the order and then kept doing it both during and after the order. That does not change the practical situation now that the order has been expired for four months.

You can document the dates, times, and exactly what is said or done (video from your own property if it is legal where you are, written notes, witnesses). Repeated targeted slurs and whistling can be reported as harassment to the sheriff’s office if you want an official record. Whether that leads to anything depends on what they actually document and whether a prosecutor or judge later treats it as a pattern.

What usually makes these across-the-street situations worse is any response from your side—looking, speaking, gesturing, or typing. Even after an order expires, a new complaint can be filed and a new order requested. The cleanest way to limit that risk is still zero engagement: no eye contact, no comments, no reactions when you get the mail or come and go. The hypocrisy is real in the sense you describe; it does not give a free pass to restart the cycle.

the judge that approved the restraining order ended up recusing because of bias and I have been to court 15 times total 3 different courts
A judge recusing for bias and the case moving across three courts over 15 appearances shows this has been a long, messy dispute with procedural complications. Recusals happen when a judge decides they cannot be impartial; it does not automatically invalidate every prior ruling, but it can be part of the overall record.

None of that changes the current status you have described:

The restraining order expired about four months ago and has not been described as renewed.
The related charges are being dropped with no plea.
A written threat still exists in the history.
The neighbors continue whistling and using the slur from across the street.
Those facts sit alongside the recusal and the multiple court trips. The procedural history (bias recusal, venue changes, repeated appearances) can matter if anything new is filed, but it does not require or reward restarting direct interaction now. Documenting ongoing conduct from your own property remains an option if you want a fresh official record; responding to it does not.

The combination of an expired order, dropped charges, a prior recusal, and continued behavior from the other side is what you are working with. What happens next still depends on whether either household creates a new incident.

that seems about right, I mostly ignore them but they do need to get a life instead of whistling at grown men and staring at them, they would do that women too, they have a "bullying" mentality they believe they can do this to anyone they want and they are putting up christmas lights while doing this to neighbors

Living directly across the street means you will still see and hear things; the whistling, staring, and comments can continue whether or not they are also putting up Christmas lights. If the whistling and slurs stay frequent enough that you want an official record of the post-expiration conduct, written notes with dates/times (or video taken from your own property) are the ordinary way to do that. Anything beyond documentation—comments, gestures, prolonged eye contact—gives them something new to complain about.

the grandma psychologically abused them they used to have cps visitations at 2030 lonnie lane

text:
🗞️14 November 2026 | Daily Edition: Saturday Afternoon

20 developments stood out through the day, spanning Bitcoin's continued weakness around $66K, persistent long liquidations, mining stress, stablecoin lending outflows, ETF flows, DeFi security, Indian banking rails, Ethereum development, Cosmos liquidity migration, prediction-market regulation and corporate Bitcoin treasury risk.

1⃣ Bitcoin made another lower low around $66K

Bitcoin perpetuals traded down toward approximately $65.9K-$66.2K, after holding closer to $66.7K earlier.

Open interest declined roughly 6.6% over 24 hours, while funding remained slightly positive.

The immediate structure now places $66K as the battleground, with $68K and then $70K becoming increasingly important recovery levels.

🖊️ Market significance: Leverage is being reduced, but positive funding suggests long positioning has not been completely cleared. Falling open interest lowers liquidation risk, but it does not by itself create new demand.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The market is deleveraging, but I still do not see enough evidence that spot demand is replacing the leverage being removed. A move back above $68K would improve structure, but I would need stronger liquidity and flow confirmation before treating it as a genuine stabilization.

2⃣ Another concentrated long-liquidation wave hit the market

One live market feed recorded approximately $47.8M of liquidations within a single hour, with roughly 97.5% coming from long positions.

Across the latest rolling 24-hour period, approximately $357M was liquidated on the exchanges tracked by the provider, with almost 89% coming from longs.

Exact totals vary between platforms because exchange coverage and rolling windows differ.

🖊️ Market significance: Longs continue to be flushed even after Friday's much larger deleveraging event, showing that speculative positioning has not fully normalized.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The persistence matters more than the absolute liquidation number. If traders keep rebuilding leveraged longs while spot demand remains weak, the market can continue producing repeated liquidation waves even after open interest has fallen substantially.

3⃣ Bitcoin mining difficulty dropped 9.13%

Bitcoin mining difficulty declined from approximately 148.36T to 134.82T at block 975,744.

The 9.13% adjustment is the largest reduction since June and follows two previous increases of 5.54% and 5.92%.

The decline indicates that block production had slowed relative to target, consistent with meaningful hashrate leaving the network.

🖊️ Market significance: Stress is beginning to appear beyond trading markets and inside Bitcoin's production economy. Lower difficulty improves conditions for miners that remain online, but the magnitude of the adjustment shows that a meaningful amount of mining capacity exited.

🗨️ My viewpoint: I do not see the adjustment itself as a Bitcoin security problem because the mechanism is functioning as designed. What matters is why enough hashrate disappeared to require a 9.13% reset. Miner economics are now becoming part of the broader market-stress picture.

4⃣ More than $500M left stablecoin lending markets

Across 279 tracked DeFi stablecoin lending pools, estimated net deposits declined approximately $521.3M over seven days, or around 2.1% after accounting for interest.

Sky lost roughly $199M, Aave V3 about $189M, Spark approximately $67.5M and Maple around $56.3M.

USDC deposits declined by roughly $141M, while USDe deposits fell by approximately $43M.

🖊️ Market significance: Crypto is not only losing stablecoin supply at the system level; existing stablecoins are also being withdrawn from lending markets where that liquidity would normally be deployed.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is one of the most important developments today. Stablecoin supply contracting while lending deposits also decline tells me capital is becoming more defensive. I want to see both stablecoin issuance and productive deployment improve before becoming materially more constructive on liquidity.

5⃣ XRP ETFs recorded their largest weekly withdrawal in around eight months

U.S. spot XRP funds recorded approximately $19.13M of net outflows during the week ending November 13.

It was the second consecutive negative week, while Friday itself accounted for roughly $1.09M of withdrawals.

XRP also fell below $1, although much of the decline in ETF asset value came from price depreciation rather than redemptions.

🖊️ Market significance: ETF demand is not strong enough to offset the broader deterioration in risk appetite, although the absolute withdrawal remains relatively modest.

🗨️ My viewpoint: I would treat this as a warning signal rather than a structural conclusion. What matters is whether the outflows persist. ETF flows become much more informative when they develop into a sequence rather than a single weak week.

6⃣ Kava disclosed a security incident involving Kava Lend

Kava reported abnormal activity involving Kava Lend in which KAVA was transferred to BNB Chain and sold.

The team said the incident was isolated to Kava Lend, had been contained and was not an infinite-mint exploit.

Further technical details remain pending.

🖊️ Market significance: The immediate risk depends on whether the incident exposes a localized vulnerability or a broader weakness in contract permissions, controls or protocol architecture.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Containment is positive, but I would not consider the issue resolved until the attack path and full financial exposure are explained. In DeFi, reassurance should follow technical evidence, not substitute for it.

7⃣ Upbit placed KAVA on its delisting watchlist

Upbit placed KAVA under review and suspended deposits and withdrawals following the Kava security incident.

KAVA also experienced significant volatility around the event.

The incident has therefore expanded from a protocol-security issue into an exchange-access and liquidity issue.

🖊️ Market significance: Exchange restrictions can fragment liquidity and make it more difficult for users and market makers to move assets efficiently during periods of stress.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The Kava situation now needs to be judged across three layers: technical remediation, exchange access and market liquidity. Even if the exploit is contained, confidence is not fully restored until all three normalize.

8⃣ JustLend began the orderly shutdown of its stUSDT lending market

JustLend is disabling new stUSDT supply and borrowing as part of an orderly market offboarding process.

Existing positions remain manageable during a transition period, after which parameters will be adjusted toward final closure.

Users are being encouraged to withdraw supplied stUSDT and repay outstanding borrowings.

🖊️ Market significance: An orderly shutdown is very different from a protocol failure. The key issue is whether users can unwind positions without generating bad debt, liquidity stress or forced selling.

🗨️ My viewpoint: I see this as controlled risk reduction rather than a negative market event. DeFi infrastructure should be judged not only by how products launch, but by whether they can be retired safely when the underlying asset or market is no longer viable.

9⃣ Coinbase India INR withdrawals remained unavailable

Coinbase India's INR withdrawal service has remained unavailable for more than five days.

Coinbase attributes the disruption to an outage affecting its banking partner rather than its own exchange or blockchain systems.

INR deposits, UPI and bank-account linking continue to operate, while users have been advised not to initiate withdrawals until the issue is resolved.

🖊️ Market significance: The incident highlights how centralized crypto platforms remain dependent on traditional banking infrastructure even when their blockchain and exchange systems are functioning normally.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is a reminder that crypto infrastructure risk does not stop at the blockchain. Reliable fiat settlement remains just as important as custody, trading and wallet operations for an exchange to function properly.

🔟 Banking-rail problems widened across Indian crypto exchanges

Coinbase is not the only Indian platform facing operational disruption.

Unocoin continues rebuilding infrastructure following its security incident, while ZebPay has also reported slower INR withdrawals linked to banking-partner issues.

The causes are not identical, but all three cases expose dependence on conventional financial infrastructure.

🖊️ Market significance: Weakness in fiat settlement can reduce market access even when crypto-native infrastructure continues functioning normally.

🗨️ My viewpoint: For India, adoption should not be measured only by trading volume or account growth. Reliable banking connectivity, deposits and withdrawals are part of the infrastructure. Until those rails become more dependable, the ecosystem remains operationally constrained.

1⃣1⃣ Ethereum developers proposed shared proof verification and sponsored batching

Ethereum developers published a draft proposal allowing multiple transaction claims to share a cryptographic proof while preserving separate payments, signatures, nonces and receipts.

A sponsor could pay the shared proof-processing cost while individual transactions cover their own claims.

The design builds on the LEANSTARK framework reserved in EIP-8288.

The proposal remains a draft pull request and has no finalized EIP number, activation date or gas schedule.

🖊️ Market significance: If implemented, the design could improve transaction efficiency and allow applications to subsidize part of the computational burden for users.

🗨️ My viewpoint: I find the direction strategically interesting, but I would not assign economic value to it yet. The important transition is from proposal to standardization, implementation and measurable efficiency improvement. Until then, this remains infrastructure research rather than an adoption event.

1⃣2⃣ Injective's Veyra upgrade received more than 99% support

More than 99% of participating Injective stake currently supports the Veyra upgrade.

The upgrade targets institutional tokenization, privacy and cross-chain trading infrastructure.

The governance vote is expected to conclude within roughly two days if current support holds.

🖊️ Market significance: The vote provides overwhelming governance support for Injective's strategic direction, but approval itself does not prove that the upgrade will generate adoption.

🗨️ My viewpoint: More than 99% support makes passage highly likely. The real question starts after approval. I want to see whether Veyra produces measurable liquidity, tokenized assets, trading activity and institutional usage rather than simply stronger technical architecture.

1⃣3⃣ More than $80M of Cosmos-linked USDC could migrate toward Injective

Approximately $84.6M of USDC.n remained on Noble as of November 11, including around $69M within the dYdX ecosystem.

Cosmos Hub has already moved its own treasury position away from Noble USDC toward Injective-issued USDC.

dYdX governance is considering moving its USDC routing from Noble to Injective through its v9.9 upgrade.

Circle plans to wind down direct Noble USDC support in January 2027.

🖊️ Market significance: This is an infrastructure migration rather than simply a liquidity-incentive story. A shift in USDC routing could change where settlement liquidity concentrates within the Cosmos ecosystem.

🗨️ My viewpoint: I consider this more important than the governance headline itself. Infrastructure becomes strategically valuable when other ecosystems begin depending on it. The key metric is how much stablecoin liquidity actually migrates to Injective and remains there.

1⃣4⃣ https://t.co/VHSKc3RFNX transferred another 64,666 SOL to Kraken

https://t.co/VHSKc3RFNX transferred approximately 64,666 SOL, worth around $5.2M, to Kraken.

The SOL originated from platform fee revenue.

Onchain estimates place cumulative https://t.co/VHSKc3RFNX SOL sales at approximately 5.6M SOL, worth close to $890M, at an average sale price near $158.

An exchange deposit does not prove that the latest batch was immediately sold.

🖊️ Market significance: Recurring conversion of native-token fee revenue can create structural supply, particularly when the underlying asset is already trading in a weak liquidity environment.

🗨️ My viewpoint: I would treat this as recurring potential supply rather than an isolated bearish event. https://t.co/VHSKc3RFNX has a commercial reason to monetize revenue. The real question is whether organic SOL demand remains strong enough to absorb that recurring selling pressure.

1⃣5⃣ MEGA cut approximately 20% of staff and expanded its AI strategy

MEGA, the organization behind MegaETH, reduced its workforce by approximately 20%.

The restructuring affected employees across blockchain, wallet, ecosystem and communications roles, while founders and core engineers remain.

The organization has also committed around $30M toward new products, particularly AI infrastructure, and plans to launch a public AI inference marketplace in December.

🖊️ Market significance: MEGA appears to be shifting from primarily building an Ethereum Layer 2 toward building commercial products on top of its own infrastructure.

🗨️ My viewpoint: I would not automatically interpret the staff reduction as deterioration. The important question is whether MEGA has found a stronger commercial use for its infrastructure or is pivoting because the original Layer 2 opportunity has become harder to monetize. Usage and revenue from the AI marketplace should tell us more.

1⃣6⃣ The CFTC directly sued Louisiana over prediction markets

The CFTC filed federal litigation against Louisiana after state action affected more than 30 companies connected to federally regulated derivatives markets.

The agency argues that Louisiana is interfering with the CFTC's exclusive federal jurisdiction over derivatives and event contracts.

Louisiana has become the 12th state the CFTC has sued over event-contract jurisdiction.

🖊️ Market significance: The prediction-market industry is moving into a direct federal-versus-state regulatory conflict that could determine whether event contracts operate under a national derivatives framework or remain exposed to individual state gambling laws.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is one of the most structurally important developments today. Prediction markets need clarity over which regulator actually controls the product. Until courts resolve the jurisdiction question, operators will continue facing a fragmented legal environment even as the category grows.

1⃣7⃣ Meta began internally testing a prediction-market product

Meta is internally testing an application called Takes, allowing employees to make predictions using non-monetary "cred" points.

No real money is involved and no public launch has been confirmed.

The experiment comes as real-money platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket continue expanding while facing regulatory scrutiny.

🖊️ Market significance: Prediction-market mechanics are beginning to attract mainstream technology platforms even outside regulated wagering and financial markets.

🗨️ My viewpoint: I see this as evidence that the prediction-market format may become larger than betting or trading. The mechanism itself can be used for information aggregation, engagement and collective forecasting. I would not assume Meta plans to compete directly with Kalshi or Polymarket, but the design is clearly moving toward the mainstream.

1⃣8⃣ Trump Media faces a potential $1B Bitcoin-treasury financing problem

Up to $1B of Trump Media convertible bonds mature on November 30.

The company's shares are trading around $4.64 compared with a conversion price of $34.72, giving bondholders little economic incentive to convert into equity at current prices.

Trump Media held approximately $1.36B of cryptocurrency assets at the end of Q3 but only around $395M of readily available cash and short-term investments.

The company is considering cash and credit financing alternatives.

🖊️ Market significance: Falling Bitcoin prices can expose financing structures built around corporate crypto treasuries by reducing balance-sheet flexibility at the same time debt obligations come due.

🗨️ My viewpoint: I would not assume Trump Media will sell Bitcoin, but this is exactly the type of second-order effect I watch during large drawdowns. The November 30 maturity creates a direct interaction between crypto prices, refinancing conditions and corporate liquidity.

1⃣9⃣ Bitcoin miners in Paraguay face growing competition from AI

Paraguay's state utility plans to allow special crypto-mining electricity contracts to expire on December 31, 2027 rather than automatically extending them.

Bitcoin miners currently consume roughly 944 MW and pay approximately $350M annually for electricity.

At the same time, Paraguay has signed a 15-year electricity agreement for an AI data-center project.

Utility engineers have also proposed limiting combined mining, AI and data-center allocations to 700 MW and auctioning available capacity.

🖊️ Market significance: Bitcoin miners and AI data centers are increasingly competing for the same scarce resource: large amounts of inexpensive, reliable electricity.

🗨️ My viewpoint: I see this as a structural issue rather than a Paraguay-specific story. The strongest miners may increasingly be those that control long-term energy relationships, because AI operators can compete for the same power with larger capital commitments and potentially more attractive contracts for utilities.

2⃣0⃣ A dormant 2011 Bitcoin wallet moved 75 BTC after being named in a lawsuit

A Bitcoin wallet dating back to 2011 moved 75 BTC, worth roughly $5M, after approximately 15 years of inactivity.

The address had been named in an unusual lawsuit seeking control of approximately 3.8M BTC across 39,069 dormant addresses.

The lawsuit argues that wallets inactive for five years or longer contain abandoned property.

The wallet also spent the small Bitcoin payment previously used by lawyers to deliver notice of the lawsuit onchain.

🖊️ Market significance: The movement demonstrates why blockchain inactivity cannot automatically be interpreted as abandonment or proof that an owner no longer controls an address.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The legal theory matters more than the 75 BTC movement. A dormant address may represent lost keys, long-term holding, estate planning or deliberate security practices. Inactivity proves that a wallet has not moved. It does not prove that the property has been abandoned.

🗨️ My Overall Viewpoint:
The market remains under pressure despite substantial deleveraging. Bitcoin has moved toward $66K, leveraged longs are still being liquidated and stablecoin lending markets lost more than $500M over seven days.

The weakness is also beginning to appear beyond trading markets. Bitcoin mining difficulty fell 9.13%, XRP ETF flows remained negative and corporate balance sheets with large crypto exposure are becoming more sensitive to falling asset prices.

At the same time, the infrastructure side of the industry continues progressing. Ethereum development remains active, Injective is positioning itself for a larger role in Cosmos stablecoin settlement, prediction markets are moving deeper into mainstream technology and regulatory structures, and DeFi protocols continue adjusting risk and product architecture.

I remain defensive on price and liquidity, but constructive on infrastructure. The immediate market problem is still that capital is leaving faster than durable demand is returning. I would need to see Bitcoin reclaim $68K-$70K alongside improving spot demand, stablecoin liquidity and institutional flows before treating a rebound as a meaningful change in the market regime.

text:
Is Fable 5.2 worth it over Opus 5.5 for everyday work?

Claude Fable 5.2 costs exactly twice as much per token as Claude Opus 5.5, and Anthropic's own launch post calls Opus 5.5 "our strongest daily driver." Yet on Artificial Analysis, Fable 5.2 at Medium effort averaged 55 seconds on single-request workloads while Opus 5.5 at Medium took 93. So which one should be open on your screen from 9 to 6: the cheaper default, or the stronger model that sometimes finishes first?

This piece covers daily use: chat, writing, coding sessions, agents, waiting time, cost and failure modes. Every number comes from a source listed at the end, read November 15, 2026.

What is identical, so you can stop comparing it

Much of the spec sheet is the same, so the choice is never about capacity:
Context window: Fable 5.2 1M tokens, Opus 5.5 1M tokens
Max output per request: Fable 5.2 128K, Opus 5.5 128K
Knowledge cutoff: Fable 5.2 June 2026, Opus 5.5 June 2026
Thinking: Fable 5.2 adaptive and always on, Opus 5.5 adaptive and always on
Effort levels: both offer Low, Medium, High, Xhigh and Max

The defaults you get without touching anything

In Claude Code, both Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 start at Medium effort. Anthropic's launch post says Medium is also the default in the Claude apps. On the raw API it differs: Fable 5.2 defaults to High and Opus 5.5 to Medium. API users who never set effort are comparing Fable at High with Opus at Medium.

No plan makes Fable the default in Claude Code. You pick it with /model fable, and it needs Claude Code v2.1.321 or later.

Speed: where the waiting actually happens

All figures here are from Artificial Analysis, which ran both models at every effort level.

Time to first answer token, matched effort:
Low: Fable 5.2 8.7 s, Opus 5.5 5.4 s
Medium: Fable 5.2 10.4 s, Opus 5.5 17.1 s
High: Fable 5.2 27.9 s, Opus 5.5 30.4 s

End-to-end time, mean of single-request workloads:
Low: Fable 5.2 49.8 s, Opus 5.5 63.7 s
Medium: Fable 5.2 55.3 s, Opus 5.5 93.1 s
High: Fable 5.2 81.1 s, Opus 5.5 120.8 s

Time per Intelligence Index task:
Low: Fable 5.2 5.6 min, Opus 5.5 3.1 min
Medium: Fable 5.2 7.4 min, Opus 5.5 6.9 min
High: Fable 5.2 15.5 min, Opus 5.5 9.3 min

The two views disagree usefully. On a single request at the same effort, Fable often finishes sooner. On longer multi-step tasks, Fable does more work and Opus finishes first.

In the Slack agent test covered below, Opus had a median response of 23 seconds and a 90th percentile of 48. Fable had 52 seconds and 1 minute 43.

Both models offer fast mode on the API, with up to 2.5x output speed at double the price. Fast Opus costs the same as standard Fable.

What a normal day costs

List prices per million tokens:
Standard: Fable 5.2 $8 in and $40 out, Opus 5.5 $4 in and $20 out
Batch API: Fable 5.2 $4 and $20, Opus 5.5 $2 and $10
5-minute cache write: Fable 5.2 $10, Opus 5.5 $5
Cache read: Fable 5.2 $0.20, Opus 5.5 $0.20

A simple API example, my arithmetic at list price, not a measurement. Take 80 chat turns in a day, each with 3,000 input tokens and 800 output tokens, no caching. Opus 5.5 costs $0.028 per turn, or $2.24 for the day. Fable 5.2 costs $0.056 per turn, or $4.48. That assumes equal token use, which flatters Fable: Anthropic says Fable 5.2 thinks before almost every reply at High and above, and a prompt asking it not to deliberate did not stop it at Medium and above.

Measured cost per task on Artificial Analysis, matched effort:
Low: Fable 5.2 $3.10, Opus 5.5 $0.98
Medium: Fable 5.2 $3.80, Opus 5.5 $2.45
High: Fable 5.2 $9.08, Opus 5.5 $3.46
Xhigh: Fable 5.2 $14.83, Opus 5.5 $6.05
Max: Fable 5.2 $26.54, Opus 5.5 $10.04

At matched effort, Fable costs 1.6x to 3.2x more per task. The more useful comparison is matched score. Fable at Low scored 54 on the index against Opus at High with 52, for $3.10 against $3.46. Fable at High scored 62 against Opus at Max with 59, for $9.08 against $10.04, and in 15.5 minutes against 25.5. From Opus High upward, there is a Fable setting that matches or beats it for less. Below Opus High there is not, because Fable's cheapest setting already costs more than Opus at Medium.

One cache detail for API builders. Anthropic measured Fable 5.2 on a 20-issue triage job. With no pauses, the 5-minute cache cost $2.18 per session. When every turn came after a 6-minute pause, the 5-minute cache expired each time and the session cost $20.36. The 1-hour cache cost $2.61 on the same schedule. If a human takes breaks between turns, use the 1-hour cache.

Where Fable 5.2 actually earns the price

1. Factual recall and admitting uncertainty. On AA-Omniscience, which rewards correct answers and penalizes confident wrong ones, Fable 5.2 at High scored 64 against Opus 5.5 at High with 42. Even Fable at Low scored 63. It is the biggest gap between the two models.
2. Hard reasoning. On HLE-Diamond at Max, Fable scored 80.2% against 67.9%. On CritPt v2 hard subset at Max, it was 76.5% against 68.0%.
3. Judgment calls inside agents. In the Deepnote agent benchmark, Fable 5.2 was the strongest model of all twelve on Decide tasks, which ask for comparing options and recommending a next step, and it was stronger than Opus at Diagnose, which asks for a root cause.
4. Digging until it finds the real evidence. In one Deepnote task, Fable compared report tables itself, found a mismatch and scored 10 out of 10. It took 1 minute 49 seconds, 34 tool calls and $4.67. Opus never opened the linked report, ranked by a health score and scored 7, in 39 seconds with 15 calls for $0.826.
5. Long, checkable work. On Anthropic's internal agentic coding benchmark, Fable 5.2 at High was the only setting above 93%, with 93.5% against 91.1% for Opus at Xhigh. On Remote Labor Index, which is vendor-reported, Fable at High scored 41.3% against 21.3%.
6. Fewer fallbacks and refusals in an independent suite. On the Vals Index, Fable 5.2 had a 1.88% fallback rate and 0.00% refusals. Opus 5.5 had 2.68% and 0.87%. Vals ran Fable at High and Opus at Max, so treat this as indicative.
7. Charts and screenshots of data. On Chartography with no tools, a vendor figure, Fable scored 73.4% against 64.4%.
8. Honesty behaviors. Anthropic's behavioral audit of Mythos 5.2, the same underlying model as Fable 5.2, found lower rates of hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming a task was done, omitting important information and hiding lazy work than Opus 5.5. Vendor finding, sibling model.

Anthropic's Claude Code docs say Fable investigates before acting and verifies its own work more often. They advise describing the outcome, not the steps, and skipping reminders to test.

Where Opus 5.5 is still the better pick

1. Anything where someone is waiting. Opus at Low gets its first answer token out in 5.4 seconds.
2. Office deliverables and briefs. On AA-Briefcase, Opus at Max scored 1801 Elo against 1785 for Fable at Max, and at High it was 1682 against 1677. On GDP.pdf, Opus at High scored 28.8% against 21.8%.
3. Legal and tax work in Vals: Legal Index 72.37% against 69.17%, Tax Agent Bench 44.54% against 32.09%.
4. Screenshots and UI mockups into code. On SWE-bench Multimodal in Vals, Opus scored 70.21% against 62.29%.
5. Ordinary coding with a clear spec. On a 463-problem SWE-bench Pro subset that Anthropic measured, Opus at Medium solved 93.1% for $0.22 per solved task. Opus at Xhigh solved 96.5% for $0.75, level with Fable at High (96.3%, $1.39). In my same-prompt test this week, both passed 162 of 162 hidden tests, and Fable cost 2.15x as much and took 29.8 seconds against 24.1.
6. Knowing when to stay quiet. When a background agent should not have posted at all, Opus held back 8 times out of 10 and Fable 6 times out of 10.
7. Coordination. In the Deepnote benchmark, Opus was stronger at coordinating teams and explaining how things work.
8. Batch jobs. On the Batch API, Opus 5.5 supports up to 300K output tokens per request with a beta header. Fable 5.2 stays at 128K.
9. Data rules. Fable 5.2 requires 30-day data retention and is not available under zero data retention unless Anthropic expressly authorizes it.

Writing: different voices, not a clear winner

Writing has the weakest evidence. Fable 5.2 has no score yet on the LMArena text board. Opus 5.5 at High is fourth there at 1507, with a margin of 6.

An Artificial Analysis personality test compares the two at Max. Judges picked Fable as more natural sounding 75% of the time. They picked Opus as more lexically varied 93% of the time and more metaphorical 80% of the time.

Fable reads plainer, Opus reads richer. For docs and release notes, Fable's voice may suit you. For copy and narrative, Opus has the measured edge. Anthropic also says Fable follows style rules closely, and a hard sentence-length limit can make its prose choppy.

Background agents: what the Deepnote benchmark says

Deepnote's Agent Initiative Benchmark, released November 13, is the closest thing to a daily-use test for an always-on agent. Each model watches a synthetic company's Slack with 11 connected services, decides whether to help, digs for evidence, then posts or stays silent. It covers 50 situations at High effort with a 180-second budget.

Score out of 10: Fable 5.2 8.17, Opus 5.5 7.84
95% interval: Fable 5.2 7.34 to 8.89, Opus 5.5 7.14 to 8.46
Cost per task: Fable 5.2 $1.87, Opus 5.5 $1.28
Median response time: Fable 5.2 52 s, Opus 5.5 23 s
Tool calls per task: Fable 5.2 20.9, Opus 5.5 10.0
Helped when help was needed: Fable 5.2 40 of 40, Opus 5.5 40 of 40
Stayed silent when it should: Fable 5.2 6 of 10, Opus 5.5 8 of 10
Perfect 10 scores: Fable 5.2 18, Opus 5.5 14
Zero scores: Fable 5.2 4, Opus 5.5 2
One month of one company's Slack: Fable 5.2 $4,684, Opus 5.5 $3,196

Deepnote's summary: Fable makes twice the tool calls, takes twice the time and costs 47% more for a score 4% higher. The intervals overlap.

For a live thread bot, Opus is faster, quieter and good enough. For background digests and decisions, Fable's digging bought more perfect scores, with more zeros and unneeded messages.

Failure modes you will hit in a normal week

Fable 5.2 stopping early. On long multi-step tasks, Fable sometimes ends a turn with a list of what remains, an offer to continue, or a stop at an ordinary obstacle. Anthropic says this happens more often at Low and Medium, and Medium is the Claude Code default. For long jobs, run Fable at High or tell it plainly to finish the whole task.

Fable 5.2 not fixing what it finds. In Anthropic's tests on small coding tasks, when the prompt did not say who owned the code, Fable tended to build on the existing structure and report nearby problems instead of fixing them. Say "you own this code, fix what you find" when that is what you want.

Fable 5.2 thinking on easy questions. Lower the effort for quick questions instead of prompting around it.

Fable 5.2 subagent bills. Fable delegates readily, and subagents can be a large share of session cost. CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL keeps them on a cheaper model.

Fable 5.2 output cap trap on the API. In Anthropic's tests with max_tokens at 16,384, 85% of Fable 5.2 attempts were cut off and it solved 20.3% of tasks. At 64,000 it solved 77.4%. Opus at 16,384 solved 57.6%, so the cap hurts Fable far more.

Opus 5.5 stopping at the first plausible answer. In the Deepnote example above, it never opened the linked report. On evidence-heavy questions, raise effort or name the sources to check.

Opus 5.5 at Low on open-ended work. Anthropic measured a big drop at Low on its internal coding set, 74.8% against 86.6% at Medium. Use Low only with a checker such as tests.

Safety fallbacks. Fable requests flagged in cybersecurity and biology fall back to another model, Opus 4.8 or Opus 5 on the API.

Switching models mid-conversation

Fable 5.2 can read thinking blocks from Opus 5.5, so moving a conversation up from Opus to Fable keeps the earlier reasoning on the Claude API. Moving down from Fable to Opus drops Fable's reasoning for the turns that run there, because no model except Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 reads Fable 5.2's thinking blocks.

The practical rule is to start a task on Opus and escalate to Fable if it struggles, rather than starting on Fable and dropping down. Changing models also rewrites the prompt cache, while a per-message effort change keeps it.

If you build your own requests, Fable 5.2 returns a 400 error when anything before a thinking block has changed. Claude Code and the apps handle this for you.

Plans and access, as facts

Free: neither Fable nor Opus.
Pro and Team standard seats: Opus 5.5 is included. Fable runs on pay-as-you-go usage credits. During launch week, Fable is included up to 50% of weekly limits, plus one Fable reset, until November 16 at 11:59 pm PT, which is November 17 at 1:29 PM IST.
Max, Ultra and premium seats: Fable is included up to 50% of the weekly limit, and it uses limits faster than other models. Past that, you continue on usage credits or switch models. Launch resets, one to three depending on how long you have subscribed, expire March 8, 2027.
Enterprise usage-based and API: standard API rates.
Claude Code on Pro shows "Requires usage credits" on the Fable row in the model picker. In non-interactive mode (claude -p), it bills credits without asking, so check scripts before pointing them at Fable.

My day with each

A typical engineering day, with the pick and why. These are recommendations built from the numbers above, not a new test.

1. 9:00, inbox triage and quick questions: Opus 5.5 at Low. First token in 5.4 seconds, and nobody needs deep reasoning to sort email.
2. 9:30, a factual question you will act on, such as a library's behavior or a spec detail: Fable 5.2 at Low or Medium. Omniscience 63 to 64 against Opus at 39 to 42 is the largest gap between the two models, and Fable Medium answered single requests faster than Opus Medium.
3. 10:00, standup notes and a status email: Opus 5.5 at Medium. Short writing, someone is waiting, and Fable's thinking adds nothing you can see.
4. 10:30, a Claude Code feature with a clear spec and tests: Opus 5.5 at Medium. The SWE-bench Pro subset gave 93.1% for $0.22 per solved task, and in my test Fable matched its pass rate at 2.15x the cost.
5. 11:30, the same feature fails tests twice: rerun on Opus at High. Anthropic measured Low or Medium with failures rerun at High at about 97% solved, for about $0.17 and $0.24 per task.
6. 12:30, the bug survives that: switch to Fable 5.2 at High in the same session. Escalating from Opus keeps the reasoning, and Fable High was the only setting above 93% on the internal coding set.
7. 14:00, a long design doc or quarterly brief: Opus 5.5 at High. Briefcase and GDP.pdf both lean Opus.
8. 15:00, reading a 300-page contract or document set for inconsistencies: Fable 5.2 at High if accuracy decides it, Opus 5.5 if it needs a polished deliverable. Fable leads on recall and reasoning, while Opus leads on Vals Legal at 72.37 against 69.17.
9. 16:00, turning a Figma screenshot into a component: Opus 5.5. Vals measured SWE-bench Multimodal at 70.21% against 62.29%.
10. 16:30, a chart or dashboard screenshot to explain: Fable 5.2. Chartography was 73.4% against 64.4%, a vendor figure.
11. 17:00, a Slack bot that answers teammates live: Opus 5.5. A median response of 23 seconds, and 8 of 10 correct silences.
12. 18:00, an overnight migration or refactor agent with a test suite: Fable 5.2 at High with max_tokens at 64,000 or more. This is the long, checkable work it was built for.
13. 18:30, a batch of 5,000 tickets to classify by morning: Opus 5.5 or a cheaper tier on the Batch API. At $2 and $10 per million tokens, Fable's premium buys nothing without evals that prove it.

Count the picks: Opus takes 8 of 13 outright, Fable takes 4, and one depends on the deliverable. Fable's slots are the ones where a wrong answer costs the most.

Side by side

Price per million tokens: Fable 5.2 $8 in and $40 out, Opus 5.5 $4 in and $20 out
Default effort on the API: Fable 5.2 High, Opus 5.5 Medium
Default effort in Claude Code and the apps: Fable 5.2 Medium, Opus 5.5 Medium
AA Intelligence Index at High: Fable 5.2 62, Opus 5.5 52
AA Intelligence Index at Max: Fable 5.2 65, Opus 5.5 59
AA cost per task at Medium: Fable 5.2 $3.80, Opus 5.5 $2.45
AA single-request time at Medium: Fable 5.2 55.3 s, Opus 5.5 93.1 s
AA-Omniscience at High: Fable 5.2 64, Opus 5.5 42
AA-Briefcase at Max: Fable 5.2 1785, Opus 5.5 1801
GDP.pdf at High: Fable 5.2 21.8%, Opus 5.5 28.8%
Vals Index: Fable 5.2 71.31% at High, Opus 5.5 70.14% at Max
Vals SWE-bench Multimodal: Fable 5.2 62.29%, Opus 5.5 70.21%
Deepnote agent score: Fable 5.2 8.17, Opus 5.5 7.84
Deepnote correct silences: Fable 5.2 6 of 10, Opus 5.5 8 of 10
Deepnote median response: Fable 5.2 52 s, Opus 5.5 23 s
LMArena text: Fable 5.2 not ranked, Opus 5.5 4th at 1507
Batch max output: Fable 5.2 128K, Opus 5.5 300K with beta header
Plan inclusion on Pro: Fable 5.2 usage credits after launch week, Opus 5.5 included

Decision checklist

Ask these in order and stop at the first yes:
1. Is it a quick reply where speed matters more than precision? Use Opus 5.5 at Low or Medium.
2. Is it a batch that can wait until tomorrow? Use Opus 5.5, or a cheaper tier, on the Batch API.
3. Is it a polished document, a legal or tax deliverable, or a UI screenshot? Use Opus 5.5 at High.
4. Will you act on a factual answer, and would a confident wrong answer hurt? Use Fable 5.2 at Low or Medium.
5. Is it a long agent run with a test, spec or other check at the end? Use Fable 5.2 at High, with max_tokens of 64,000 or more.
6. Has Opus 5.5 at High already failed a check you can repeat? Escalate to Fable 5.2 at High in the same conversation.
7. Is it a decision or root-cause question that needs digging across sources? Use Fable 5.2.
8. None of the above? Use Opus 5.5 at Medium.

Two more rules apply in every case. Never run either model at Max by default, because Fable's Max costs 2.9x its High for 3 more index points, and Opus's Max costs 2.9x its High for 7. And when you change your mind mid-task, move up from Opus to Fable, not down.

The verdict

For everyday work, Fable 5.2 is not worth it as a default, and it was never meant to be. Anthropic says to start on Opus 5.5. The measured gaps on writing, office deliverables, UI code and quick answers either favor Opus or are too small to pay double for. And Opus has the better instinct for staying quiet in an agent.

Fable 5.2 is worth it as a deliberate second gear. Switch to it when being wrong costs more than the token bill: factual answers you will act on, decisions, root causes, long agent runs with a finish line, and anything Opus has already failed. On the Artificial Analysis index, a Fable setting matches Opus's top settings for less money and time. In a 13-task day, that is 4 or 5 Fable tasks. The rest belong on Opus.

What this comparison does not settle

Artificial Analysis figures were read November 15 and are recomputed every few days, so speed numbers move. Deepnote is 50 tasks at one effort level, and the intervals overlap. Vals ran Fable at High and Opus at Max.

The SWE-bench Pro subset, internal coding set, output-cap and cache studies are Anthropic measurements. Remote Labor Index, Chartography and the audit are vendor-reported. Anthropic publishes no token figures for plan limits, so Fable's drain rate has no official ratio. The cost example and the 13-task day are illustrations, not measurements.

8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An
@NPR
  reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook
