Here’s mine, Mechanic! 💫

Delin Windsong is the Shieldblade and Aetherblade Maiden, one of the last surviving members of the Vaelari race. Though not biologically related to her companions, she and the other surviving Vaelari refer to each other as sisters because of their shared bloodline and the near extinction of their people. The bond between them is all they have left.

At the age of eleven, Delin’s home city was attacked by the Infusans. Her father, Arden, tried to escape with her through the old sewer tunnels below the city. As they fled, they were spotted by Infusan soldiers. Arden was gunned down while shielding his daughter. Delin fell into the river below with her father’s lifeless body. In that moment, she uncovered one of her signature shield spells. A magical body barrier that forms on her entire body protected her from the impact, saving her life.

She washed ashore alone and pulled herself out of the water. Nearby, she found the body of a fallen Vaelari warrior and a ceremonial dagger. Hearing tortured screams coming from a hut, she followed the sound and witnessed a nightmare. Inside were three Infusan soldiers tormenting three young Vaelari girls named Iris, Sky, and Rose, all around ten years old.

The Infusans had mutilated them. Iris’s fingers and toes had been severed. Sky’s teeth had been ripped out. Rose’s face had been doused in acid, leaving her blind in one eye and badly burned. The soldiers were laughing as they continued the torture. One of the men removed his helmet, revealing his skin.

All Vaelari females are born with a unique ability called Essence Drain, a racial trait that activates through direct skin contact. Delin used the opportunity to grab the unarmored Infusan and triggered her Essence Drain. Her eyes turned red as she absorbed his strength, overwhelming and killing all three soldiers with the dagger. The three girls were saved, and from that moment, they stuck together.

The four escaped the town and eventually reached a collapsing bridge with Infusan soldiers closing in. At the last moment, a man named Kade appeared, singlehandedly destroying the enemy squad. He led the girls to an abandoned castle deep in the wilderness. There, they began to recover and train.

Kade appeared as a savior but he harbored a dark secret. He had willingly submitted to a spirit walker, believing it would grant him the power to protect others. Instead, it took control of him. These spirit walkers require only verbal consent to possess a host, and they choose those with strong bodies and fragile minds.

Over time, the three girls named Sky, Rose, and Iris became hardened and vengeful. The trauma they endured warped them. Though still young, they began to embrace a darker path. Delin, however, remained committed to justice and compassion. She rejected vengeance, even while the others began to follow Kade’s twisted ideals.

Delin’s inner strength made her an outlier. She questioned Kade, stood her ground, and began to distance herself from him and the others. Her bond with her sisters grew strained. Though she understood their pain, she refused to let it consume her. She remained the only one among them to resist corruption.

At a later point in the story, Delin is mortally wounded by an Infusan sniper during a quest for the artifact. As she lays dying, a spiritual entity appears and offers her power in exchange for control. The player is given a choice: accept the deal and take the dark path, or resist. If Delin resists, her collected elemental relics awaken. The final two relics, light and dark, manifest and unlock her true artifact weapon, Despair’s Requiem.

Delin’s story is one of loss, endurance, and choice. She fights not for revenge, but to protect what little hope remains in a world scarred by suffering. Her strength was born from what she refused to become. Her debut arrives in late 2027-2028.

Combat Style

Delin has two combat specializations.

One focuses on shield-based defense, protection magic, and precise counterattacks. The other transforms her sword into a massive two-handed weapon, channeling absorbed essence into devastating strikes.

LYON COUNTY, Nev. (News 4 & Fox 11) — State investigators determined Lyon County Sheriff Brad Pope did not break any laws when he created a fake Facebook profile and leaked confidential case information during his campaign for sheriff in 2022.

News 4-Fox 11 obtained a redacted copy of the investigation through a public records request. The story was first reported by the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

The investigation, finished in January 2023, concluded that Pope did not violate laws regarding interference with an investigation, official misconduct or possible interference with an election.

The public comments and messages posted from a fake Facebook profile by "Hank Tyme," later identified as Brad Pope, leaked information regarding the details of murder suspect Troy Driver's 2022 suicide attempt.

One message sent to News 4-Fox 11 sought to undermine then-Sheriff Frank Hunewill, Pope's opponent in the 2022 election, by accusing him of covering up the suicide attempt without a proper investigation.

Comments from Tyme included calling Hunewill dishonest, incompetent and a joke. One accused Hunewill of dismissing complaints about Driver's suicide attempt to make it 'go away.'

Hunewill, who spoke with News 4-Fox 11 via Zoom Tuesday, said he couldn't publicize Driver's suicide attempt because it was privileged information about an inmate in his care.

The information was posted to a Facebook account by the name of "Hank Tyme." Investigators found the photo used in the profile was of a lawyer from Maryland.

The Lyon County Sheriff's Office, through Facebook search warrants and a T-Mobile warrant, found that the phone number connected to the Facebook account was almost certainly that of an LCSO employee.

The phone number was only used to make a few calls, including one to Sheriff Hunewill's wife where the caller requested personal and financial information, according to the investigation.

No charges for Lyon County Sheriff Brad Pope after leaking case information on fake profile during 2022 election
by Ben MargiottTue, January 2, 2024 at 4:05 PM
LYON COUNTY, Nev. (News 4 & Fox 11) — State investigators determined Lyon County Sheriff Brad Pope did not break any laws when he created a fake Facebook profile and leaked confidential case information during his campaign for sheriff in 2022.

News 4-Fox 11 obtained a redacted copy of the investigation through a public records request. The story was first reported by the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

The investigation, finished in January 2023, concluded that Pope did not violate laws regarding interference with an investigation, official misconduct or possible interference with an election.

The public comments and messages posted from a fake Facebook profile by "Hank Tyme," later identified as Brad Pope, leaked information regarding the details of murder suspect Troy Driver's 2022 suicide attempt.

One message sent to News 4-Fox 11 sought to undermine then-Sheriff Frank Hunewill, Pope's opponent in the 2022 election, by accusing him of covering up the suicide attempt without a proper investigation.

Comments from Tyme included calling Hunewill dishonest, incompetent and a joke. One accused Hunewill of dismissing complaints about Driver's suicide attempt to make it 'go away.'

Hunewill, who spoke with News 4-Fox 11 via Zoom Tuesday, said he couldn't publicize Driver's suicide attempt because it was privileged information about an inmate in his care.

"It was disappointing because I felt that he was still better than that," Hunewill said.

Just goes to show you that some people will do just about anything to try to achieve their personal goals.
Then-Sgt. Pope defeated Hunewill in the campaign for Lyon County sheriff later that year by just 968 votes.

As of 4 p.m. on Jan. 2, 2024, Pope had not responded to multiple calls and emails seeking comment sent early Tuesday.

The Lyon County Sheriff's Office launched an investigation after it was determined that confidential information only known by LCSO employees regarding Driver's suicide attempt was made public.

The information was posted to a Facebook account by the name of "Hank Tyme." Investigators found the photo used in the profile was of a lawyer from Maryland.

The Lyon County Sheriff's Office, through Facebook search warrants and a T-Mobile warrant, found that the phone number connected to the Facebook account was almost certainly that of an LCSO employee.

The phone number was only used to make a few calls, including one to Sheriff Hunewill's wife where the caller requested personal and financial information, according to the investigation.

Though Pope's name was redacted in the released report, investigators wrote that the subject of the investigation won the election and was the new sheriff of Lyon County.

After the election, the Nevada State Police major crimes unit determined that certain elements of the Nevada Revised Statute regarding disclosure of information to subject of investigation were not met.

"Due to the fact that there are no relevant charges that could be identified that would warrant further investigation of this case this case is closed," the report states.

🧊 $NVDA’s ICEBERG 🧊 @nvidia’s off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantees just hit $530.5B, up about 10x in five quarters. The balance sheet shows only $91B of liabilities. Here is the breakdown. 👇

📊 The math (10-Q, quarter ended July 26, 2026, Note 10): $366B ordinary commitments + $56B additional commitments + $108.5B guarantees = $530.5B. SemiAnalysis (@SemiAnalysis_) first tallied it on September 11.

🧩 The pieces:
Supply and capacity: $279B, up from $119B, mostly memory. 🧠
OpenAI Ohio lease guarantee: $105B. 🏗️
Neocloud take-or-pay: $36B. ☁️
Data-center leases: $20B. 🏢

🧠 Why it matters:
Nvidia is no longer just selling chips. It is increasingly backstopping the AI buildout, including @OpenAI’s Ohio campus and neocloud partners. When customers’ leases lean on your guarantees, sales and risk become entangled.

⚖️ The fair counterpoint:
These are maximum gross exposures, not expected losses. The Ohio guarantee covers defined portions of lease and power payments, starts to matter when leases commence (first site in fiscal 2029), and comes with an OpenAI indemnity. SemiAnalysis frames the loss case as neoclouds failing while Nvidia’s own cash flow slows.

📏 Scale check:
$530.5B is about 5.8x total liabilities of $91.3B and roughly 2.3x shareholders’ equity of $229B.

🗓️ Next catalyst:
Tuesday 11/17 after the bell: Nvidia’s Q3 FY27 report, Colette Kress’s first as interim CEO. Listen for commentary on commitments, guarantees and cash generation.

SemiAnalysis says this could grow past $1 trillion if Nvidia keeps leaning on its cash flow. A bigger backstop book means a bigger headline risk if AI demand wobbles.

Three things I will watch Tuesday:
1️⃣ Does the commitment total keep climbing or stabilize?
2️⃣ Any new guarantees, or more detail on Ohio and neocloud exposure?
3️⃣ Memory costs and gross margin, since supply commitments are mostly memory.

Bottom line: Nvidia’s cash machine is becoming the AI economy’s backstop bank. 🏦

Berkshire is sitting on $356.9B of cash and T-bills.

1% of SpaceX costs $18.9B.

That's about 5% of the pile.

I think there's a decent chance Berkshire is quietly building a SpaceX position.

It may have already started. I can't prove it. Monday's 13F can't either. It only shows what Berkshire held on 30 September, six weeks ago.

And Berkshire has hidden positions before. In 2024 it built a Chubb stake in secret. The SEC let it keep the stake off its filings for months. The 13F finally showed 25.92M shares, worth $6.72B, on 15 May 2024.

Today Berkshire holds more cash than stocks. $356.9B against $335.5B.

Berkshire owns Alphabet. Alphabet owns about 4.1% of SpaceX. So today Berkshire's slice is indirect. About 0.035% of SpaceX, around $670M.

What if Greg Abel wants more than the indirect slice?

SpaceX just went from a $541M loss to a $4.40B net profit in one quarter. So here are five things Buffett looks for in a business. SpaceX passes four. It still fails one.

1. The moat

Buffett, 1995 letter: "economic castles protected by unbreachable 'moats.'"

On the Q3 call Elon said SpaceX flies almost 90% of all the mass that goes to orbit. China is about 6%. His numbers, not an audit.

I don't see anyone crossing that moat this decade.

2. Pricing power

Buffett, 2010: "the single-most important decision in evaluating a business is pricing power."

In early November Starlink switched to pricing by how crowded your area is. In the busiest US areas it's going up as much as 20%, from the first bill on or after 30 November. Residential Max goes from $130 to $156. In empty areas it goes down.

It's on the order page. Check your own area.

Buffett says a weak business has to have "a prayer session" before raising the price by a tenth of a cent.

Starlink is raising it $26 a month in some places.

3. The toll road

Everyone who wants to reach orbit pays SpaceX. Now everyone who wants compute does too.

Anthropic's S-1 lists up to $120.5B of compute from SpaceX's AI business through 2029. Anthropic starts trading on Thursday 19 November.

Rockets, internet, compute. Three toll booths, one owner.

4. The owner is the operator

Elon can't sell a single share until mid-June 2027. About 6.4B shares.

The only way he gets paid is SpaceX getting more valuable.

Buffett, May 2025: "I have no intention, zero, of selling one share of Berkshire Hathaway."

Both bosses are staying in the boat.

5. The one it still fails

Buffett, 2007 letter: the worst business "grows rapidly, requires significant capital to engender the growth, and then earns little or no money. Think airlines."

Q3 was SpaceX's first profitable quarter as a public company.

Net profit was $4.40B. Operating income was $2.79B. Over nine months, free cash flow is still about -$35B.

Most of the spending is AI buildout. $16.4B of the $19.6B it spent in Q3.

SpaceX's CFO said on the Q3 call that new compute pays back in under a year at current pricing.

If that holds, the last box flips too.

The price

IPO $135. Peak $225.64 on 16 June. Low $120.39 on 5 November. Friday's close $139.11.

Revenue went from $7.8B in Q2 to $14.6B in Q3.

Buffett, 2008: "be greedy when others are fearful."

On 5 November SpaceX fell 9% in one day. Everyone was fearful.

$1,000 in Berkshire

Now zoom out 60 years.

Buffett took control of Berkshire in 1965. Back then it was a failing New England textile mill.

Berkshire's own 2025 letter tracks the share price from the end of 1964 to the end of 2025.

$1,000 became about $61 million.

That's 19.7% a year for 61 years. The same $1,000 in the S&P 500, dividends included, became about $462,000.

And it didn't go up in a straight line. In 1974 Berkshire fell 48.7%.

Berkshire and SpaceX look alike

Both looked broken early. Berkshire was a failing textile mill. SpaceX's first three rockets failed.

Both fell hard. Berkshire dropped 48.7% in 1974. SpaceX dropped 47% from its peak to the 5 November low.

Berkshire was the 60-year compounder.

SpaceX could be the next one.

$1,000 in SpaceX

$1,000 at the $135 IPO is about $1,030 at Friday's close.

That's day 155. Berkshire is year 61.

I'm not saying SpaceX turns $1,000 into $61M. Nobody gets to say that on day 155.

My guess: day 155 will look as early as 1965 looks now.

Monday 16 November, Berkshire files its 13F.

That's the list of stocks it owned on 30 September. Six weeks old.

Three things can happen:

1. No SpaceX on the list. That proves nothing. It's an old snapshot.

2. SpaceX on the list. That's the headline.

3. A line that says "confidential treatment requested." That means Berkshire is buying something it isn't ready to show yet. That's what it did with Chubb in 2024.

I'm watching Monday's list, and the ones after.

Moat: yes. Pricing power: yes. Cash flow: next.

Sounds crazy I know, its the ultimate boomer company but if I was Berkshire , I would buy at least 1%, literally nothing to lose by doing that and a lot to gain.

text:
This evening I received a text so long I thought a company had accidentally sent me its employee handbook, annual report, and the director’s cut of its unresolved feelings. 

It was from a company I mention often. The message, in essence: stop tagging our name, or else. OR ELSE? Sir, I write about hiring. I didn’t steal the Declaration of Independence. I read it twice. Not because I was intimidated, but because I was searching for the part where the author offered me a job. After all, if you have time to compose a novel about my LinkedIn posts, surely somebody has five minutes to reply to a candidate. Priorities, people. A text threatening consequences gets same day delivery; an applicant asking for an update gets sent into the Bermuda Triangle with a PDF resume.

Apparently, I have committed the unforgivable corporate sin of using the name of a company while discussing its hiring practices. I assumed that was how conversation worked. You mention a business, you discuss an experience, and everyone moves on. But somewhere, someone saw a tag and reacted like I’d launched a submarine in their conference room. I can picture the emergency meeting: legal on line one, communications on line two, and a VP whispering, “Has anyone tried making the process better?”

Let’s be clear: I don’t wake up plotting how to ruin somebody’s Tuesday. I wake up, drink coffee, and read stories from people who are exhausted by a system that treats their time like it’s free and their dignity like it’s optional. Then I write. Sometimes with jokes. Sometimes with anger. Sometimes with both, because apparently sarcasm is the only department still responding within 24 hours.

And yes, it stings. Not the warning itself. It’s realizing how quickly a company can find the words to tell someone to be quiet, while so many people wait weeks for a few words about whether they still have a shot at a job. Imagine the energy we could save if just a fraction of that urgency went into treating applicants like human beings instead of abandoned shopping carts.

Maybe speaking up costs opportunities. Maybe it makes people uncomfortable. I know the risks. There are nights when I wonder whether I should just post motivational quotes about synergy, compliment every CEO’s leadership journey, and call a four month hiring process an exciting adventure. It would probably be easier. I could even sell mugs: SILENCE IS GOLDEN, ESPECIALLY DURING RESTRUCTURING. But then another person writes to say, “Thank you. I thought I was the only one.” And that matters more than a corporate approved smile.

So to the company texting me tonight: I hear you. I won’t invent stories, and I don’t expect anyone to agree with every word I say. But asking questions and sharing opinions aren’t crimes against the quarterly earnings call.

And if your next message is another five page thriller, please include a plot twist, a decent ending, and an actual human response to the people applying for jobs. They’re still waiting.
